posts.caption:
Mudang primarily work with a pantheon of 신 shin we usually refer to as our 신령님 shinryungnim. It's our shinryungnim who open the doors to various abilities, specialities, and types of rituals and ceremonies we can do as mudang

Our shinryungnim can be a mix of celestials, deities, bodhisattvas, saints and other types of gods, in addition to, our own defied ancestors. This is a big part of why what one mudang does might not work for another mudang, and won't work for those who are not initiated mudang. Central to our practices is our relationship with our own unique pantheon that no other mudang has

We also work with gods outside of our own pantheon when that is required to help our clients

At the end of the day, being a mudang is a closed practice. It's a tradition that is embodied through the historical traditions that were found on the Korean peninsula, but the core of mudang lineages is from the spirits

Ancestors do not select the mudang, the gods do. We in turn, have a responsibility to care for the world and all sentient beings. That often requires a mix of oral traditions passed down to us through our lineage elders, adaptation and resourcefulness in the face of an ever changing world, and inspiration from our shinryungnim 

It's an immense responsibility, and we aren't picked because we are "perfect." Being a mudang necessitates that we are human first. There is no mudang who is not human, and the more fully we embrace our humanity, the better healers and guides we become

posts.caption:
Holding energy and holding space to start the lunar new year 😊 Big energy doesn't have to be used right away, and it doesn't need to be explosive

Gym time lately, has been about muscular endurance and working on stabilizing muscles. Sustained movements and isometric holds is what I've been working in to my training during this block

Big energy can turn into big stagnation and blockage too. Just because it's a lot of energy, doesn't mean it will flow. It can wear you out (both by ripping through you or by getting stuck and causing a big 'traffic jam') if you're not mindful. Moving your body is a really straightforward way to move your energy

Holding potential energy. Controlling and sustaining tension. Solidifying my foundation. Preparing for more explosive movements. That's how I've decided to harness Fire Horse energy in a seemingly mundane way during my gym time

How have you been doing this 1st lunar month of 2026? 😊

posts.caption:
If you've spent time with a strong femme person who cares for you, and is real with you, you likely understand more about Mother Mary than any canonical text could reveal to you

Femme narratives have too often been edited and presented through a man's perspective. Femme narratives have too often been presented in ways that make them convenient 

How could dogma, doctrine and the words of men who want to celebrate women only when they're convenient, and put them in their place when they are inconvenient, be expected to show us the fullness of divine feminine? 

The feminine is always part of the masculine, and the masculine is always part of the feminine. You see, they were never separate to begin with, but elements of a whole. We need both, regardless of how we identify. A healthy relationship with both energies is important

Trans, non-binary, agender, femme, masc, woman, man... No matter how you identify, every person has what we understand as feminine and masculine energies, and we need them both for spiritual balance. We become stiff and fragile when our energies are not allowed to be dynamic and in harmony 

Feminine is not always saying "yes", and never saying "no" 

Feminine is not forcing yourself to smile and be pleasant while you bury your true feelings

Feminine is not shutting down your critical thinking 

To be clear, these things are not masculine either

These are all unhealthy methods of teaching people to neglect their needs. Saying "yes" to everything, forcing ourselves to be pleasant, and shutting down our critical thinking makes us convenient, "easy" people, but they are not what defines the feminine, nor the masculine

posts.caption:
I started the energetic year of the Fire Horse working with fire in ritual. I was reminded that fire burns what is flammable. Period. 

Fire demands respect, awareness and one who is willing to listen 

A fire that is not listened to becomes an uncontrollable blaze, burning and deconstructing things into mere carbon remnants, indiscriminately 

A big portion of the files have been released--and though this event takes on a triumphant tone for many, it should be sobering, too 

We are reminded once again, that victims and survivors in the U.S. are rarely centered. Their information and stories disrespected, even in the process of seeking truth and justice 

We are all burning 

As a SA survivor, the entire process leading up to the files being dropped has been wrought with many thoughts and emotions. I too, felt triumph at the news that the files had dropped. I also felt pain 

I felt worry for those who may be retraumatized or triggered in various ways by the continuing influx of SA and human trafficking content flooding their feeds and news. If you are, please take time for yourself. As much time as you need. Making content can wait. Reading the files can wait (indefinitely). That is the most revolutionary thing you can do for yourself. In a system that constantly cuts and inflicts trauma based on a time table, please heal. Don't rush. Take your time. Do what you need to do to be present. Set and maintain boundaries. Surround yourself with those that help you process, when you are able to. Community should ground you in lived reality. Your existence and its reality matters 

For those who may not be able to empathize with survivors, I humbly ask you to consider our realities before you speak on the files. Ending cycles does not mean erasing a circle entirely, but rather, breaking a circle so that it can spiral into a different plane from 2D to 3D. Often, well meaning words can inflict the same traumas and perpetuate the very cycles they mean to break. They can end up erasing one circle only to unknowingly copy and paste it elsewhere, instead of transforming it. So please speak, but be wise. I believe in you

A blaze will burn everyone indiscriminately

posts.caption:
With Korea being in the northern hemisphere, this day is observed as the winter solstice. On 동짓날 Dongji, it’s traditional to make 팥죽 red bean porridge. The red bean porridge is first served to the gods of the home, the ancestors, and then to the living who reside at the home 

Another tradition is to fling red bean porridge outside the home or to smear it by the entrances, as it’s thought this will scare away lowly spirits during the long night of the winter solstice. Alternatively if you don’t have red bean porridge you can throw plain red beans or put bowls of red beans at places you would have smeared porridge on (like by your front door) 

The winter solstice marks the turn of the season from autumn to winter, metal to water, Sagittarius to Capricorn. It’s a day naturally dominated by yin energy, and a good time to move slowly and gently. Finding the path of least resistance and flowing like water, rather than blasting through moments with intensity and vigor

Happy Dongji! May you find rest in the darkness and warmth by the fire 🕯️

posts.caption:
Winter solstice is called dongji 동짓날 in Korean. It was regarded as the beginning of the year long ago. We also have January 1st, Ipchun 입춘, and Seollal/Korean New Year 설날. Each one having been regarded as some kind of beginning — a new year — at some point in time

These days can serve as a time for endings, beginnings, as a doorway, times of new or renewed momentum, and so on…

Connecting to ancestral traditions looks different for everyone. If you’ve ever felt invited to observe one of these days more than the others, it could be a nudge from the ancestors you have the strongest connection to

Alternatively, perhaps you feel nudged to observe traditions on January 1st, even though it’s not “traditional.” This could be your ancestors encouraging you to adapt. It’s a good reminder that traditions can be observed in many ways, and what’s practical for us as their descendants should be taken into consideration too

For those in the northern hemisphere, winter solstice is quickly approaching this weekend, while the summer solstice is quickly approaching for our friends in the southern hemisphere. However you spend the solstice, may it be everything you need for the year ahead!✨

posts.caption:
✨What Do Mudang Do?✨ 

Our main purpose is to help beings, including human beings! 

That can come in the form of blessings and protection for children, undoing knots and twists of fate/course correction, blessings for the success of businesses, helping ghosts pass on to the afterlife, providing spiritual consultation for life matters, one year life forecast readings, general divination and prophecy, banishing lowly spirts from houses, exorcisms, blessing movie sets, making protective and empowering amulets for athletes and fighters, etc. 

The mudang tradition is an indigenous folk tradition. We adapt to situations and make adjustments as we go. What we do involves thinking quickly on our feet. This is  a big reason why an apprenticeship period is necessary for mudang. Even for quick-learners, there really is no substitute for the invaluable lessons of time and experience

________

posts.caption:
✨Mudang & Korean culture✨

Mudang have been shaped by, and have helped shape, Korean culture for thousands of years. A semi-traditional or hyper-traditional lineage mudang ceremony (굿) may give people a glimpse into parts of Korean culture that have faded away in mainstream culture (specific elements of clothing, symbols, colors, etc.)

At the same time, mudang traditions are very much their own thing. Let me explain…

We may use traditional instruments like 장구 janggu and 징 jjing, but we play them in a music style that is specific to mudang music

You might see traditional Korean symbols of certain flowers and animals on our clothing, both they may hold a slightly different meaning for mudang

We may use Korean as our main language of worship, but even the use of certain words in a mudang context differs from how they would be used otherwise

So, although our traditions are Korean, they’re specifically Korean in a mudang way

You won’t find details about our traditions in books because it’s a closed practice. Scholarly research tries its best to describe our traditions with what information is available to them, but it’s always good to remember the value of consulting an actual mudang if you have questions about what we do 😊

________

Shot and edited by @shinobichenault

posts.caption:
✨Mudang work with all kinds of spirits✨

We have a pantheon of deities we serve at our personal shrines. These are the gods — that include deified ancestors — who are the source of our abilities and talents as mudang

We often work with the ancestors of our clients too. Whether it’s relaying direct messages to their descendants, or working with them to help our clients, ancestors are high on the list of spirits we work with!

Mudang are intimately tied to nature and the land, so we also tend to work with the spirts of the land that we’re on. This does not mean we work with spirits that are from other closed traditions (Ex. Native closed practice deities), but that we interact with the local spirits in a respectful way

posts.caption:
Families can be complex. Ancestors can be complex. 

Being mixed is something that was looked down upon for a myriad of reasons, and it’s not surprising. When existence is political, the existence of mixing can seem threatening. One may wonder, where are the boundaries and “rules” that kept identities separate and tidy? 

…But would it be so radical to sit with the discomfort first, rather than acting out on what triggered discomfort? 

Would it be so radical to lean into someone’s identity and humanity, rather than how their existence threatens your comfort? 

It takes a lot of individual and collaborative work to heal past cycles and make sure wisdom continues to be transmitted through the generations

It can feel impossible at times to push through. Like we have too much on our plate, but can’t figure out what to do

Do we find a bigger plate? Maybe we should just find a huge tray? Do we eat faster? Do we invite more people to eat with us? Should we cut off the source of food? Is that possible? 

[And perhaps I love food, which is how we find ourselves with this analogy 😆]

All this to say… There is a way. It’s not often going to be easy with families and ancestors. It’s going to look different for everyone, but the heart we act with is what matters most

posts.caption:
✨Tools of the trade

To those who don’t know, a mudang’s tools might just look like ordinary bells, fans and the like

It might seem like anyone could buy similar tools and use them. That’s not totally untrue. One who is not a mudang could buy similar tools and use them, but they wouldn’t have the same spiritual and energetic effects. Here’s why…

It’s the mudang’s gods that empower the items and channel their power through them. It’s because of this, that even though they may appear ordinary to the naked eye, energetically they are quite special and custom fit to each mudang

The same tool could have many uses that all depend on the gods that the wielding mudang has. Blessings, cleansing, purifying, banishing, focusing energy, dispersing energy, calling and sending away energies… the list goes on and on! 

Our tools are used and maintained with great care, and put to good use for a very, very long time

posts.caption:
I used to be a competitive dancer when I was younger. We’d go over our scores after competitions and there would always be one judge who was on the voice tape. We would play their tapes and listen to their critiques as a team

One time, we were listening to the tape when the judge pointed out a dancer (it was me). They told me to “open my eyes.”

Watching YouTube make-up tutorials as a teen, I quickly realized none of them were made by people that looked like me. Even the asian ones. Everyone had distinct double eyelids and bigger eyes, while I basically had no fold/crease and small eyes (this was in the early 2000s) 

It took me a few years to appreciate my own eyes. A lot of my peers who shared similar eyes ended up getting surgery, or using double eyelid glue or tape to achieve the double eyelid look. I tried the tape once and quickly realized I didn’t like it on myself. I didn’t look like ME 

So, even though I didn’t like how others felt about my eyes (and I couldn’t figure out how I wanted to wear eyeliner for a while 😆), I kept my eyes just the way they were

One day, well into my 20s, I looked in the mirror and realized how much I’d grown to love my eyes. It wasn’t just acceptance, but I really embraced and appreciated them. Somewhere along the way, I’d stopped caring what others thought about them, and that allowed me to love myself without disruption

If there’s parts of you that you love, but feel pressured to change because of what others think and say, LOVE YOURSELF ANYWAYS. Don’t let other people ruin the love you could be showing to yourself 🫰🏻

#happychoharu #happynewmoon

To get a glimpse into the tapestry of fates underlying this world is truly amazing. Some things are nearly set in stone, while other things can be softly reoriented or reshaped. Sometimes they can be rewoven, too

I know that I know nothing at all 😆 I trust my shin 신령님 to help me navigate these things a mere mortal could never do over and over again. Without their guidance, I really wouldn’t be able to do many of the things I’m able to do now 🙏🏻

On another note, sometimes people will say they’re not spiritual or “tapped in.” Yet, these same people will innately know how they should pray for someone, or what intentions they need to send to someone in any given situation

If someone has fallen ill, they’ll know whether to pray for a speedy recovery versus a smooth and peaceful passing. If someone is struggling to get a new job, they’ll know to pray for the removal of obstacles in their way versus praying for more opportunities for work. These can seem like small things, but this is how being “tapped in” can look too

So, just know that being tuned in to energy, spirits, etc. can look different for everyone 😊

posts.caption:
Some more photos from the Chuseok festivities!

House gods and ancestors are all spirits that lay people in Mugyo can work with! In the first photo, I’m offering a humble Chuseok spread to a house god called “성주 sungju” 

In the second photo, I’m 음복 fevering the offerings that had been made to the ancestors during our Chuseok 차례 charye (ancestral rite). The offering spread had included various dishes including 송편 songpyeon, 전 jjun, 나물 namul and 토란국 toranguk

In Korean, we technically don’t say we “work” with gods or ancestors. We say “모신다” [mo-shin-da]. This means we keep someone we respect or hold in high esteem close to us, caring for them and serving them. This emphasizes our relationship with gods and ancestors, rather than obligation or transactional exchanges

Baekjung 백중날 is a lesser known full moon day of offering. You can do a charye 차례 (ancestral rite) on this day, earnestly making offerings to your ancestors and praying for blessings and health as we prepare for the Fall and Winter months

In a few weeks, we’ll get to celebrate Chuseok 추석, which is the better known day on which many families used to travel far distances to gather in one place, and offer a big charye 차례 

Baekjung always falls on the full moon of the 7th lunar month. This year, it coincides with the effects of the lunar eclipse in pisces, providing a powerful opportunity to lock-in with our ancestors and guides

2025, for many reasons, has been a major time of awakening. Many things have been revealed to the world and in our personal lives too. The next few months will be no different 

There will be things that are out of our control. Perhaps more than ever before. Be okay with loosening your grip on how you think things should be and trust the process. Trust in the preparation and work you’ve been putting in, both intentionally and unintentionally in your practice 

May our intuition be sharpened by each and every revelation 🙏🏻

posts.caption:
There’s nothing wrong with changing paths

Some have a path that entails they’ll be dedicated to a single practice, religion, or philosophy their whole lives. Others may never feel drawn to make any of these aforementioned things a big part of their lives. There’s also those who might find themselves switching over to a different framework of practice after having dedicated years of their life to the study and practice of another

Converting or finding out that we’re called to walk a different path years down the line doesn’t mean that we messed up by not choosing the right path the first time. Sometimes it’s just about timing 

It’s okay to honor the communities, spirits and practice that gave us so many experiences and lessons, even if we’re no longer practicing the religion 

Just because a religion, spiritual practice or lineage isn’t right for us at this time, it doesn’t mean it does not hold value for anyone else. In fact, it can still hold value for us after we’ve stopped practicing it, just in a different way than when we were directly involved

The practice we leave behind doesn’t have to be labeled “bad” or “wrong” and the new practice we go into doesn’t have to be “right” or “better than”

Many things can be true all at once. Sometimes a big shift in our path just means we’re being asked to make room for more of the truth 

I’ve been there, and I still often think back to the years before I was a mudang. There’s been times I just needed to sit with anger, disappointment or just flat out confusion as to why things are the way they are, and that’s okay

It’s okay to allow yourself time to process and go through the different thoughts and feelings that can come-up while going through big changes. These moments of processing might come in long seasons or as brief moments that are sprinkled throughout the years 

There might be a time  when you can look back in gratitude. A time when lessons learned in the past seemingly continue into the present in their own magical way. A time when things develop and reveal themselves in ways you never could have understood before

posts.caption:
Another term I should mention is “aedong jaeja” or “aedong” for short. This is what some might translate into English as baby mudang 😊

Aedong jaeja 애동제자 is what I am. It’s a term used to refer to young disciples who are still in the formation and development stages of learning lineage traditions

The aedong phase starts once we’re initiated, and is a critical time of learning. Aedong spend a lot of time with our spirit parent/god parent who will prepare us to become independent full fledged mudang 

Though there may be spirit-led elements of our tradition, we also have wisdom and teachings that have been passed down through the centuries. These teachings are a significant part of our practices and take time to learn well

How long someone is an aedong can really vary. It’s a little different than going to school and finishing a program within a pre-determined time frame. It’s more about determining when we are ready

At minimum, we can be considered aedong for 3-5 years. Of course, the learning never stops and will continue for the rest of our lives, but becoming a full fledged mudang means we should have built a strong foundation to our practice, and are able to make decisions independently without needing guidance from our spirit parent

Photo 2 - Onggi 옹기 tip jar

I was shopping for offerings with a good friend. We were in the produce section picking out fruits for our shrines. As we shopped, we realized our different approaches to picking out fruit offerings 

My friend tried to find the best looking fruits. They prioritized vibrant color and uniform shape and size 

I tried to find the best tasting fruits. I prioritized weight and scent 

We both avoided fruits that had broken skin and any bruises 

Even though our approaches looked different on the outside, we were doing it with the same heart. We wanted to offer the best fruits at our shrines to show our devotion and earnest commitment

Things can look really different from the outside sometimes, but if we take our time and observe for just a while longer, we can often see things that allude to what’s at the core

posts.caption:
An ancestral rite I had the honor of doing for a client’s ancestors 🙏🏻

For those who have been asking how to do ancestral veneration in the Korean style, I’ve got something in the works for you. Stay tuned for that! 

Chuseok 추석/Hangawi 한가위/Mid-Autumn Festival is coming up on October 6th. This is one of the special days when we prepare a bigger ancestral offering called charye 차례(similar to what’s pictured here) 

Though there are plenty of regional and family specific variations, one of the staple offerings for ancestral rites is called three-colored namul 삼색나물. The three symbolic colors of this dish are brown, white and green 

My family traditionally used spinach 시금치, balloon flower root 도라지 and fern bracken 고사리 for the three colors. I’ve also heard of other families using other kinds of namul instead 

Ancestral veneration is a time of remembering and honoring the wisdom of those who came before us. It can also be a time to reflect on mistakes and generational cycles that we’d like to intentionally address and meaningfully change moving forward

posts.caption:
How come Koreans have different opinions on art and media (ex. KPop Demon Hunters)? 

Well, for one, the experience of being Korean (or any other identity), is not to be overgeneralized. Every single person who identifies as Korean is entitled to their own opinions. We’re all individuals who identify by the same collective identity of “Korean”, but we have our own experiences within and outside of that collective communal identity too 

What’s cool and exciting to one person might be 촌스러워 (tacky and unrefined) to another

Upbringing and life experiences influence how we perceive things, and our local culture can influence us greatly in how we perceive things that broadly fall under the category of art 

All this to say, these different opinions are valid. Knowing what you think or how you feel about something is a good practice in knowing yourself and learning how you want to move through life

The other part of this is knowing what you’re moving through. What is the setting? What is the context? What is the reality for others? This includes learning how others view the same thing you’re viewing, whether it aligns with you or not 

How we want to move through life + knowing what we’re moving through, work in tandem and inform one another. It’s a dynamic relationship, not a static absolute

Knowing what we’re moving through requires being knowledgeable of facts too

People being unlawfully detained and deported in the U.S. is not an opinion. It is a fact 

Women’s health and reproductive rights being stripped away piece by piece in the U.S. is not an opinion. It is a fact 

Erasure of LGBTQIA+ in the U.S. is not an opinion. It is a fact 

Ongoing gen0c!de in the world 🍉🇨🇩🇸🇩 is not an opinion. It is a fact 

We can’t move through the world how we want to unless we know what we’re moving through

A mudang can have many different kinds of gods. Amongst them are child gods. Child gods can go by many different titles. 동자 dongja, 애기씨 aegi, 동녀 dongnyu, etc. 🌈

They’re mischievous, funny, silly, serious, sweet, cute, rambunctious… It really just depends on the specific child god’s personality and disposition 

My child gods are quite protective of me. They often remind me to put my foot down in certain social and energetic situations. They advise me when to walk away, or remind me to enjoy the moment when I’m being too serious. They can also get very upset when I’ve been wronged 

It’s through them that I’m reminded of how deep feelings can go, and how expansive they can be. I’m reminded to make time for my feelings and to honor them as they come

This path of being a mudang isn’t as simple as a “yes” or “no”. Having the calling vetted and confirmed by an elder doesn’t automatically mean we are going to get initiated. There’s still choice involved, and not everyone decides to accept the calling 

There are a lot of feelings to process…Heartache, desperation, loss, letting go, acceptance, motivation, jealousy, ambivalence, anger, relief, frustration, joy, sorrow, pain, contentment, hope… 

The more people choose to walk in their true power and path, the better this world will be. What that power and path is looks different for all of us

Whether your main calling in this life is to be a parent, visual artist, revolutionary, martial artist, entrepreneur, healer, spiritualist, nun, reporter, community organizer, advocate, educator… No matter what the calling, keep doing your thing 

Just because what we do is meant for us, doesn’t mean we’re obligated to feel happy all the time

Don’t be afraid to feel and feel deeply. It doesn’t have to be joy, nor does it have to be something “positive” 

Even child gods feel like doodoo sometimes😆🥲🫂

Did you know that we add a whole month to a lunar calendar leap year? 

Gregorian calendar leap years add just one day in the month of February (366 days instead of the usual 365)

2025 is a lunar leap year. Every lunar leap year, there is one month designated as the month to be repeated. This year, that month is the 6th lunar month

Instead of starting the 7th lunar month on July 25th, we’ll be going into another 6th lunar month (6B) 

In total, a lunar leap year has 13 months 

Do you know your lunar calendar birthday?

One of my history professors began the semester by going off on how poorly the U.S. education system taught history

As we went through world history, they would often remind us how the material he was teaching us as university students was taught to elementary school students in other countries

Their critique of the U.S. system, the way they taught, and even their approach to grading exams are memories I recall and continue to learn from over 10 years later

History does repeat itself, albeit a little differently each time. What determines that slightly different portion each time we return to familiar places? 

Is it knowing our history that stops us from repeating it? Is it the company we keep that holds us accountable and reminds us of our path? From a slightly different angle, does history truly repeat itself in the grand scheme? 

Can you tell I was a sociology major? (I believe we’re notorious for asking questions… and more questions🤣)

posts.caption:
I grew up in the aftermath of the LA Riots. My early experiences left me with more questions than answers. Perhaps some of you have had a similar experience? 

When I was around 9 years old, I climbed up into a tree with two other friends. We settled into the trees wide branches and talked excitedly in Korean when two neighborhood kids ran to the base of the tree and began yelling, “Ching Chong” remarks at us. They threw sticks and stones at us, one of which, landed and cut my eyelid. An elder family member who had lost their shop in the LA Riots happened to be home that day. When I returned home, they noticed my eye immediately and ran out to find the neighborhood kids who had hurt me. Back then, I didn’t know how to say it, but I knew part of my hesitancy in telling my family member what had happened, was because the kids who had thrown sticks and stones were brown and black. I knew my family member could be very discriminatory towards other POC, particularly blacks. The scars of the LA Riots ran deep for them. I knew that for them, the intent was to protect, but I couldn’t help but feel there was a better way

Fast forward to just about a week ago. I briefly stopped by a popular sandwich spot on the way to work. I needed some extra fuel and this spot sold really strong coffee. When I walked in, there was a young black man who looked like they were waiting for an order. I stood by the cash register waiting to order. The cashier walked out a few moments later calling out a to-go order and its details. This order was for the young man. He stayed silent for a while and then began to call the cashier racist for getting his order wrong when they never get orders wrong when the customer is yt. The cashier was perplexed. They were Asian. When the young man left, the cashier later pondered out loud to their co-worker how they could be racist when they too, are a minority and POC, and had tried their best to fulfill the order 

I share both of these stories to say, Asian communities are still wrestling with the tension between us and other POC groups. This discussion is relevant and will continue to be

Continued in the comments 👇

Tensions between Korean-Americans and Black? Still definitely there. Whether we choose to acknowledge it or not

There’s a lot of history that influences and informs all of this tension, but how long do we want to continue these cycles? How long are we going to let these cycles continue by doing nothing? These cycles are harmful. They hurt our communities, and also hurt other communities. In the end, no one wins

We have to start somewhere, and if that somewhere is simply you pondering thoughts and feelings that arise from reading my post today. Then so be it. That is a start. Engaging in internal dialogue with yourself as you process this is important

When you’re ready, I encourage you to also engage in continuing dialogue with people of your own communities. Then to take that and engage in continuing dialogue with other groups as well. I truly believe continuing dialogue is key. 

Not just one conversation. No, that allows us to give in to discomfort. We need to keep talking to one another. Talk through disagreements and hurt feelings. Talk through our fear and collective pain, until we arrive in a space where we can hold one another’s stories with care and collective compassion, and find a way forward together

And in this spirit, I invite you to comment and engage in dialogue here. Whether it’s sharing memories or moments where you wish you could have done better, or your experience organizing community dialogue regarding discrimination, colorism, abelism, etc. Even if it’s not perfect, or comfortable, we’ve got to talk and keep talking to one another about this.

posts.caption:
This was me. Years ago. Spirit led me out of the Roman Catholic Church, and I began the next phase of my journey. I didn’t know the exact details of what was to come. I just knew I had to move. It was a big ask

My career, ministry, volunteer work and general network of people was largely church bound or church associated back then

Being a queer person of color who presented as a woman in most church spaces, was not easy. Standing up for the youth, and putting my foot down in the face of priests and seminarians who did not understand the toxicity they spoke and enacted was difficult

The thought that honoring and respecting someone’s gender, sexual orientation, their right to choose, and standing with the marginalized were so radical that some viewed me as heretical or lost was quite astounding

Emphasis on apologetics and absolutes, rather than truly empowering people with lessons that would serve as soft skills to help them live out the heart of the gospel message was something I never agreed with
 
Through my own struggles, I learned to respect Pope Francis aka Papa Francisco so deeply. He navigated the scrutiny and pressures of the papacy with grace and humility. He brought hope and made so many feel seen. I felt seen, too 

I attended my first World Youth Day in 2016 as a chaperone. It was in Poland, and Papa Francisco gave a blessing at the end of mass to a field filled with people from all over the world. I’ll never forget that pilgrimage

My road led me away from the Church, to a place I could never have imagined for myself. Yet, no matter where I was, I found myself checking in on Papa Francisco

In my own way, here’s me holding space for Pope Francis. As a mudang. As someone living out my life to the fullest of my potential. I’m grateful for his influence in my life

Rest in peace Papa Francisco. You are loved. Thank you for opening the Holy Doors. Not just this Jubilee year, but for opening the door for so many throughout your life. You truly lived your life for the greater glory of God

AMDG 🙏🏻

곡우 Gogu is the Corean jeolgi season when people pray for rain and a fertile, strong start to the agricultural season. This is the start of the rice season when seedlings are prepared. It happens to coincide with Easter in the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches this year 

Some believe that any kind of impure energies would result in a failed or bad rice harvest, and in order to combat this, will make sure those who may have been around unclean energies are not allowed around the rice

Artemisia princeps, a mugwort native to East Asia, is called 쑥 ssuk in Korean. It’s the herb pictured here. It’s a versatile herb that we use in various culinary recipes, medicinally, and spiritually too! 

Yang energy is considered to be at its peak on 단오 Dano, which falls on May 31 this year. Dano is a perfect time to pick fresh ssuk and hang a bundle by your door for protection ✨

If you want to learn more about Corean spirituality, I’ll be giving a workshop on May 3 in Huntington Beach, CA

posts.caption:
✨오방기 

If you’ve had a session with me, you may have seen me use these colored flags 🌈

This 무구 mu-tool has become one of the most well-known representations of the mudang craft. It’s considered a closed practice tool, meaning, it is to be utilized by initiated mudang only. Though it has many uses, you’re going to be most familiar with flags as a divination tool

They will be called 오방기 ohbanggi or 칠방기 chilbanggi depending on whether they’re a set of 5 colored flags or 7 colored flags

As mudang culture becomes more popular, there are more and more videos and articles that try to explain the meaning of the flags. However, having a set of flags and doing readings based on face value definitions of each flag falls woefully short of the true depth of this mu tool 

Though the flags are a closed practice, the 오방색 5 directional colors themselves are abundantly and openly used throughout Corean culture in things like philosophy, decorations and clothing

posts.caption:
There’s no doubt that having the words to express yourself and your identity can be healing and empowering

Words can help us navigate our identities and be the catalyst for discovering new parts of ourselves. They can help us identify people who share parts of their identity with us, bringing us closer to communities and groups where we will hopefully be embraced and supported

Yet, when terms we identify with are used politically and legalistically, they can take on a more exacting tone. Though in this form they may provide potential road maps for legislative change that brings awareness and rights to communities, they can also work against those communities

So, next time you are in a conversation about why someone is NOT like you. When you feel the need to make lines distinct and perfectly compartmentalized… I urge you to consider why you’re doing it

Are you doing this to better help someone else find the right identifier words they can use to grow and learn in their unique identity? Are you doing this to respect and uplift their identity? Is it coming from a place of making space for new identities outside your comprehension? 

Or…

Are you doing this as an exclusionary act? Are you pushing them out and labeling them as “other”? Are you doing this to kick them out of your space and feel secure in your own identity? 

Words… utterance… the things we say out loud are so important in a spirit/magic/energy practice. The things we say matter outside of ritual, ceremony and obvious magical spaces. The things we say in our everyday lives are magic in it of themselves

How did you use your words today?

posts.caption:
(자동)차 고사 cha gosa AKA car spirit blessing 

This is something anyone can do for their cars or vehicles. During a gosa, you make offerings to the spirit of your vehicle. You pray they will keep you and your passengers safe and out of danger, and wish the spirit a long healthy life 

If a mudang does the gosa for you, you can expect their gods will be blessing your vehicle as well! They may also provide talismans to keep with the car after the gosa 

What offerings are made and how a gosa is done can vary depending on lineage and region, but here are some general tips if you’d like to try for yourself as a lay person…

Offer fresh water, bottle of soju or makgeolli, fruits, 씨루덕 red bean rice cake, and 북어포 dried fish 

Place offerings in front of the car and greet the spirit by bowing. Pray, and then circle the vehicle as you pour the soju on the ground around the vehicle 

You can pour the water on the vehicle gently and sprinkle some of it on the interior of your vehicle too

The offerings are considered blessed and you can eat them after the gosa 

It’s recommended you do a gosa for your vehicle when you first get it, or if it starts having issues 

Have you done a cha gosa before?

The 2nd month of the Korean year is the month of 풍신/영등신 the god of wind. They are often described as grandmother gods of the winds

During this month, it was believed that the grandmother gods of the winds came to visit. People would pray and do rituals to ask the wind gods for protection from destructive winds

Winds can be refreshing, dry, gentle, fierce and destructive. They can come from the mountains and oceans. In the philosophy/practice of 풍수 pungsu (literally “wind & water”), wind is one of two deciding factors of how one reads and interprets the energies of the land, a home, a city, etc. 

This new moon in Pisces brings about quite a wind. Gusts may threaten to push us over, or blow us far away from our goals and destinations. Huge shifts are coming. Be strong, flexible and consistent! 

Happy 초하루 choharu everyone! It’s already the 1st day of the 2nd month of the year of the snake 🐍

posts.caption:
Let’s be honest 

We live most of our lives not knowing what truly lies ahead. We may assume what’s coming next based on things like our experiences, data patterns, and advice from community

When things happen in a predictable manner that meets our expectations for the future, we feel secure and assured. We feel that we can see clearly and we know what lies ahead

When things don’t go as expected, it’s easy to start questioning what we thought we knew. We might feel things are really unclear, and we may even feel overwhelmed by the sudden change in perspective 

But really, whether things are expected or unexpected, we never truly know what lies ahead. We do, however, decide how we meet that truth 

Do we meet it with fear? Curiosity? Respect?Arrogance? Denial? 

Do we fight? Fawn? Freeze? Run? 

There’s so many ways to meet this truth, and we can meet it in any combination of ways at different times in our lives

What is incredibly helpful in this life long journey of not knowing what comes next, is community 🤝

So who’s in your community? 

Friends, family, pets, ancestors, spirits, deities? Co-workers, chosen family, online communities, wild animal friends? That one lady who walks with you to the bus stop? A stranger who donated to help you? ✨

Second Image: Photo of Hsi Lai Temple Bodhisattva Hall back lit by the rising sun, decorated for Amitabha Buddha’s Bday (17th day of the 11th lunar month) 

🌌Winter solstice is the longest night of the year. A long, cold and dark night that was thought to be filled with lowly energies. The Corean tradition of eating 팥죽 red bean porridge and spreading it around the home were methods thought to keep these lowly energies away from the family and home

Dongji AKA Winter Solstice used to be observed as the Corean New Year’s Day 

It falls on December 21 or 22 in the Northern hemisphere, and June 20 or 21 in the Southern hemisphere. Since the Korean Peninsula is in the Northern hemisphere, dongji was traditionally observed in December 

But what if you live in the Southern hemisphere? Do you  observe dongji in December or June? I’d love to hear some thoughts on this and how you’re adapting your traditional practices for your current situation and setting

As for me, I’m in the Northern hemisphere, so I’m observing dongji this weekend. I woke up before the sun was up to prepare offerings for the shrine (including the traditional red bean porridge 🫘) & spent time with friends at temple and over video calls 😊

3rd photo - Depiction of the 장산범 Jangsanbum, a trickster deity (Naver webtoon “2013 전설의 고향” ep 6)

As an animist, I encounter all manner of spirits. As a baby mudang, the spirits central to my practice are the gods who make-up my personal pantheon. They are the ones that empower, teach and guide me. They help me, help you! 

But what about other spirits? Lowly spirits that want to attach to us, stronger heavy spirits who love tricking us and causing all manner of mischief, both acute and chronic? What about all the other kinds of spirits that exist in this world and influence our lives in their own ways? 

Essentially, there are always going to be spirits that do not share the same goals as us, and have different priorities than we do. This is life. C’est la vie~ This is how it is with other humans, as well. Right? 

I respect that each spirit has their own role to play, and I stay true to my own goals and priorities. I too, have my own role to play. I set boundaries and I maintain them according to my goals, and when I encounter spirits other than my own gods, it can serve as a reminder of my own purpose

Whether out of mutual understanding and support, contrast, or conflict, these interactions often lead me to a deeper understanding of why I do what I do. Assessing myself relatively in these situations helps me understand myself better 

So, rather than getting wrapped up in fear, frustration or rigid and dichotomous judgments, especially when interacting with spirits that may test my own goals (or even threaten my own goals), I choose to take the interaction as a potential learning lesson

So what if they try to trick me? I can play the game and I will always play well as long as I stay true to my purpose in this world. It’s possible to trick a trickster, and gain much insight through that process

Have you encountered tricksters? Do you work with tricksters? What is your view on working or not working with them?

posts.caption:
Candle blooms are auspicious ✨ 

Candle blooms 촛불꽃 happen when the very top of the wick blossoms into the shape of a flower(s) while lit. Candle blooms come in many different shapes and sizes, and can vary in exact meaning. They’re usually personal messages from 신령님 our gods to us. They can also happen on ancestral altars or any other setting where spirits are communicating to us through a burning candle

When candles bloom, the way the length of the exposed wick + tip of the wick are shaped are typically much more delicate than when a wick mushrooms (which can often happen when a candle burns poorly). Candle mushrooms are usually very bulky and need to be trimmed off

Candle blooms fall off on their own, and leave behind a delicate stem. They can bloom on occasion, or bloom repeatedly one after the other on the same candle. The exactly meaning is usually personal to you and your spirits, so discern for yourself what may be being communicated to you if your shrine or altar candles bloom! 

The first candle bloom I saw after my 신내림굿 initiation was shaped like a beautiful orchid (no, I don’t have photos. I don’t take photos of everything, you know?😆) My gods affirmed my path and encouraged me to work towards certain things that were developing at the time

Do you burn candles on your altars, or do you use electric candles/lamps? Have you seen a candle bloom before?

posts.caption:
✨Shrine of 1,000 Helping Hands✨

The name of the shrine came about through months of prayer and intentional thought. In Korean hangul the shrine name is written 천아동 신당 (chun ahdong shindang), and is primarily written in hanja/Sino-Korean as 天兒童神堂. The secondary hanja is 千兒童神堂. These two hanja versions of the shrine name are pronounced the same and written the same in hangul, and serve to express a double meaning. The primary name means “Shrine of the Celestial Children” while the secondary name means “Shrine of 1,000 Children.” Fitting titles for a shrine whose tiny and powerful child gods bring so much joy, blessings and protection to the people they help 👼🏻👼🏻👼🏻

In English, Shrine of 1,000 Helping Hands serves as a translation of  the shrine’s Korean name and its reference to the many child gods present in the pantheon. It also makes reference to the 1,000 arms of Guan Shi Yin 관세음보살 that compassionately come to the aid of many. Known as Guanyin to most, this beloved bodhisattva resides at the Shrine of 1,000 Helping Hands as well, alongside many other gods who make it possible for many to be helped

Though there are limitless many who need aid, I will strive to help them all 
Though there are endless lessons of truth to learn, I will continue learning them all

With each passing year, I’ll continue to dedicate myself to cultivation and study. I may make mistakes, but I won’t make them in vain. With the help of my gods and my community I will grow stronger and more focused so I can help more and more people! 

The Shrine of 1,000 Helping Hands will grow and I pray it will be a safe haven for many throughout the years

On special days like seollal 설날 (Korean new year), I offer a little makgeolli 막걸리 to the spirits of my instruments

I put a little bit of makgeolli on a clean tissue and wipe the surface of the instrument with it to feed the spirit. I thank each of the instruments for helping me make beautiful sounds and music, and ask them to continue helping me make beautiful sounds for my gods in the coming year! I’ll also do this when I bring a new instrument home!

Mugyo is animist, so we believe that even the inanimate objects like our cars have spirit. When we “bless” cars, homes and businesses, it is actually a ritual called gosa 고사. When we do a gosa, we are making offerings to the spirit of whatever is being blessed, checking in with the spirit and asking it to look out for the person using the car, living in the home, conducting business there etc.

posts.caption:
Samjae 삼재 can be translated as “the three calamities”

Samjae is a period of 3 consecutive years that are said to bring misfortune into one’s life. To try and mitigate the effects of their samjae, people buy talismans specifically made for this purpose, and have rituals called samjae puri 삼재풀이 done at buddhist temples or by mudangs

Before you freak out, hear me out! The samjae energies interact with every individual’s fate lines a little differently. This can mean that sometimes the calamities are tiny and not very noticeable. Other samjae cycles may leave you feeling absolutely defeated. Other cycles you may actually enjoy some good fortune instead of calamities. This last one would be called boksamjae 복삼재 

For myself, I’m in my last year of samjae and it was not boksamjae this cycle 💀 So, rituals and chants were done to mitigate many misfortunes

2022, 2023, 2024 were the samjae years for those born in the years of the rat, dragon & monkey. For anyone whose with me in this cycle, our samjae will be over with the start of the lunar new year on January 29, 2025 👏

2025 will mark the beginning of samjae for those born in the years of the rabbit, sheep & pig! If that’s you, take care in 2025, 2026 and 2027. You can always have a session with a mudang to see how this samjae cycle will affect you. Some people get samjaepuri done as soon as they can, while others wait to get it done once they run into trouble. The lucky ones won’t have to worry because it’s boksamjae for them 😆

What’s your animal zodiac sign? Have you heard of samjae before?

1st day of the 10th lunar month in the year of the wood dragon 🐉 

It’s new moon (choharu 초하루) today, and it’s bewildering how so many things have changed from the last new moon ‘til now. My gods have been bringing about necessary changes in my life. A sense of calm and assuredness settles in as the way forward materializes

Thinking outside the box is a good place to start, but eventually we must come to realize that when we orient ourselves in this way, we are still living relative to the box. Not good, nor bad. Just depends on what you need 

Systems can be useful in our daily lives, for work and for our society at large. Yet there’s times we’re called to re-evaluate them and ponder their existence. 

When we don’t agree with a system, what do we do? 
When we do agree with a system, what do we do?

Each of our answers to these two questions will be unique. Some of us know exactly where we stand at this moment, some of us don’t know, and others may be in a phase of rediscovery

Whatever your plan or lack of plan, I pray you’ll end up exactly where you need to be, equipped with the tools and community to do what you need to do in this life

2024 is almost over, but we have a lot more life to live. Let’s be intentional and try our best 🙏🏻

posts.caption:
As we set-up the ocean ritual space, the surface of the water was serene and calm, like a smooth glass surface reflecting the skies above. Sometimes we think we must look upwards to find the gods and devas, but this isn’t always so. We look down to see the heavenly reflections and we look up to see the light that gives the earth its color. Openness to many perspectives and surprises are necessary in our understanding of spirits, realms and divinity 

As we began the ritual, a gentle and constant breeze blew in from the ocean. The water came to life. The Dragon King made himself known to us. Throughout the ritual, the energies continued to support, encourage, and protect us. As the Sun rose higher and higher in the sky with every passing hour, people and pets began to join us on the shore. The spirits of the land helped keep them at a safe distance, giving us more time and allowing the ritual to come to a natural close

Sometimes we worry. I know I worry a lot. I’m a natural planner and coordinator. I worry about the details and how things will come together. I tend to worry about things I don’t understand, or perceived holes in plans. I put a lot of pressure on myself to get things ready, and get things done. Yet, the gods will do, as they do. In their wisdom and foresight they guide me. I’m learning to let go when I need to, so that the gods can work

The gods will provide. The only thing we have to do is open our eyes to see, our hands to accept, and our hearts in gratitude

posts.caption:
As I sat at the jesa table I had prepared for my late grandmother, we had a conversation. One that helped me see the generational patterns and trauma that linked us together. As she revealed these things to me, I was so thankful to have shared this time with her. At the same time, my heart ached for her. For all the pain she endured and persevered through. The grief and disappointment that she had not had the proper opportunity to air while alive. Our farewell was sweet and warm. She reassured me she was well taken care of, and that she would not need jesa in the future. The Catholic offerings and prayers of my parents were enough for her. Still, we enjoyed the short time we had together as she enjoyed the jesa table I had set for her for the first and last time

Jesa is an ancestral ritual that takes place on either the night before your ancestor’s death anniversary, or on the actual day of their death anniversary. It’s an opportunity to connect with a loved one who has passed on, and to provide for them while they work through the afterlife

Traditionally, a family would have separate dish ware for these ancestral rites. Up until now, I’ve just been using what I have, hoping that one day I’ll be able to buy my ancestors nice serving wares. Then, recently I was given our family set of jesa dish wares. I was not even aware we had any. I was shocked, but I could feel my ancestors brimming with excitement. At last, proper dish wares. At last I’d figured out where to find them

As I washed each bowl and lid, I was filled with joy and excitement. Gratitude came in waves as well. What a beautiful life I have. A life where my family ties are mending before my eyes, and I’m being helped along by my gods and ancestors. These may just look like metal bowls, but to me, they’re a gift from my gods. They’re a gift from my ancestors. It’s a message that I’m on the right track and that my gods will provide for me and those I love

I’m really looking forward to using these dishes for the next family jesa. I know my ancestors are looking forward to it as well 🙂🙏🏻

September 17, 2024 🌕
This week I shared meals with my 신령님 gods, house gods and land spirits, new friends, loved ones, and ancestors. I’m thankful I’ve had such a full week surrounded by good company

It’s 추석 chuseok today. Growing up, I didn’t quite understand its significance, but I’d like to think I’m growing into it now. 

 I spent years of my life wanting to open a communal space centered around food. Whether a small restaurant or specialty coffee shop, I just knew I wanted to create a safe gathering space that would foster compassion and love of neighbor. Looking back, I wonder if it was my calling to become a mudang that had placed that desire in my heart 

This chuseok, as I shared meals with so many beings around me, I realized how my desire to share a meal with those around me has evolved and been clarified as I walk the path I’m on now. The lessons brought to me by those relationships have been tough, even overwhelming at times, but the fruits have been numerous and abundant too. 

This chuseok/mid-autumn festival, the full moon in Pisces along with the partial eclipse is definitely setting us up for what’s to come. As we now shift into the moon in Aries, many of us are in for quite a ride… But what’s life without a little adventure, right? 

Happy chuseok. Happy mid-autumn festival. May your guides and ancestors lead the way, and may you be receptive and malleable in the face of what’s to come. Things once concealed will be revealed. May your eyes not avert, and your mind be open to subvert what you once thought you knew. Let’s step into the next chapter friends 😉

Getting settled in after my renewal ceremony and processing all the blessings, messages and visitations

There are so many layers to the mundane world we see, and to the many worlds that go unseen (by most). There are periods of creation and birth, as well as, periods of destruction and decomposition that maintain the balance of this world we live in. Both are equally important and necessary

It should not be a surprise that we are currently in the destruction and decomposition part of that cycle. After many years of creation and growth, it’s time for balance, and a return to what will give birth to a new cycle of creation in the future

There was much shared about what’s to come, as many gods came down throughout my 3-day renewal ceremony. There were gods that stayed, gods who came down to voice their support, and others who let me know that they would be near

The deer came to bless me and greet me. The ladybugs came by, too! So many 방울 bells fell off throughout each day of ceremony that if I hadn’t reattached them as I went, I would have been jumping with just a bare handle (FYI a single bell falling off a mudang’s bell rattle during ceremony is extremely auspicious)

“As above, so below” - Our world will reflect the happenings of the many realms. I’m ready for what Iies ahead. For better or worse, the way forward will be made known and I will walk the path with my head held high

I was speaking to a friend the other day about how our wardrobes have changed since we got initiated into our respective traditions

I used to love wearing all black. I still prefer to wear all black when I can. Maybe a hint of color here and there, or even a pop of color if I’m feeling fancy. Even then, that “color” is usually something neutral like white, grey or tan. Nowadays I feel myself drawn to a little more color 🤭

When I’m in shinbok 신복 (god clothing) for ceremony, there is so much color. Beautiful gold threads, colorful fabrics, flowing cloaks and beautiful armor reflecting rainbow colors in the light. The energy of ceremony is vivid and colorful! 

Though I walk with one foot in the earthly and one foot in the spiritual, I am more present than I’ve ever been. Colors are more vivid, moments more heartfelt, and matters of the heart much deeper than ever before

I’m thankful I get to live this life as a baby mudang 🙏🏻

posts.caption:
I always offer a cup of coffee to my ancestors on special days. It’s roasted, ground, and brewed at home by the family, so it seems fitting to share our love and efforts in this way

Ancestral veneration is something I didn’t see much growing up. There was jesa 제사 for relatives that had passed (death anniversary tradition), but my family stopped practicing that tradition before I finished elementary school

Shout-out to my Vietnamese friends, because in their homes is where I saw my first proper ancestral altars

Nowadays, I try to do what I can for my chosang 조상 (ancestors). I know they’ve got my back and will protect me and vouch for me, and I do what I can on the earthly plane to provide things they may need in the afterlife

If you want to start a practice and you don’t know where to start, ancestral veneration is a great place to start 🕯️

Happy cho haru 초하루 🌑

On the 1st day of the 6th lunar month, history and family seem to be motifs for me

Think of family medical histories and how we can be predisposed to certain conditions through our ancestry (cancer, auto-immune disorders, etc.) 

Think of generational curses stemming from habits and mannerisms that were unknowingly, and knowingly, passed down (addictions, coping mechanisms, etc.) 

Think of wealth in all its many forms that can be inherited (financial literacy, land, money, etc.) 

Ancestry is significant. So is history. 

Everything our ancestors did happened in the context of the world around them. History is an amalgam of all of our collective ancestors and their stories

It is true that all of our ancestors contributed to the history behind us, though their stories are not equally recorded, shared nor accessed

We, too, share this plight. The plight of contributing to history every waking moment, regardless of how our stories will, or will not, be known (both while we’re alive and after we’ve passed on)

Where do I stand? What is my power? Where is my power? How will I use it? 

Where do you stand? What is your power? Where is your power? How will you use it?

Dano 단오 is considered to be the day with the most yang energy 양기. It falls on the 5th day of the 5th lunar month every year. This year it falls on June 10th. 

Yang energy is associated with the sun, light, warmth, expansion, male, and life.

If there are any areas of your life that need a lively push in the right direction, now is the time! Utilize the strong yang energy to help break habits that don’t serve you, stimulate growth and progress, and to expand your horizons. 

Like the flowers and plants that are moving and focusing their energy upwards and out into their flowers at this time, it’s time to move that energy you’ve held in your roots up into your throat chakra, and to speak your truth! 

Happy pride month 🥳

posts.caption:
“How do you learn how to be a mudang?“

My thesis work had to do with Korean-American Catholics and suggested the significance of food culture in spirituality. Of course I had to do some background research on Korean spirituality, and that was when I found out about “Korean Shamanism”

I had been raised without a mention of it until my mid-20s, when I kept reading about this “Korean Shamanism” that played such a significant role in the spirituality of the Korean people. 

All of the sources I read were written by academics and scholars. None were written by Korean shamans. A majority were written from an ethnographic or theatrical/performative perspective. 

Many of the articles felt like recycled information I had read in other articles. There was usually some mention of the gut ritual 굿, shinbyeong 신병, initiation 신내림굿, and the stigma associated with mudang 무당. 

Fast forward many years after writing my thesis, and I’m now an initiated apprentice. I’ve realized how much more there is to Korean Shamanism AKA mugyo 무교

There are so many more kinds of rituals and workings that we do beyond the gut ritual. There are so many different styles/ lineages of mudangs. Stigma is also such a nuanced thing rooted in a specific cultural and social context. I’m finding out what that means, or doesn’t mean for me day-by-day as Korean diaspora. 

How do you learn how to be a mudang? 

Before anything else, you need to confirm you have a calling to be a mudang by being vetted by an elder shaman. Sometimes this can mean being vetted by elders of traditions outside of mugyo (if you do not have access to mudang elders). This is especially true for the Korean diaspora populations. Then you find the right spirit mentor who will initiate you into their lineage.

I learn tradition that is specific to the lineage I was initiated into through my spirit mentor. These traditions are only passed down to initiated spirit family members. Then there are the lessons I learn directly from my shin 신령님 AKA gods.

Following initiation, it is through tradition & spirit family, our shin, constant effort, and time that we learn how to be mudang.

I was running around, trying to help prepare things for 굿 grand ceremony. I was tired and a little overwhelmed, but I was really pushing to learn as much as I could throughout the prep. 

When I went to change out of my 한복 hanbok, I noticed the  butterflies at the bottom of my skirt were gone. My mental processing speed was very low from lack of sleep, but it finally hit me after a few seconds— my skirt was inside out 🫠

It had been inside-out the WHOLE time. Before, during and after 굿 grand ceremony. It’s little humbling moments like this when I realize (1) it’s time to check-in with myself and (2) get some rest. Also, ended up not being a big deal because it looked fine, but it was just funny finding out AFTER we had been in ceremony for hours 🤣

So anyways, my skirt is inside-out in this photo. Thanks for taking a nice photo of us @that.korean.witch 🫰🏻

posts.caption:
Humble offering this new moon 초하루. Sweet potato leaves and loquats from the garden, and assorted goodies from the grocery store and Mayday Faire this past weekend. 

As a child, I prayed a lot. In my own humble, small way. When I’d be in unbearable pain, in a hopeless situation, or harassed by frightening spirits, I would pray. I would pray sincerely and from the heart. I didn’t know how to ask people for help, but I would pray to the divine to come to my aid. 

As I got older, my relationship changed with prayer. I began to prioritize logic and action. I wondered what good prayers were if they did not move us into action. I wanted to be the change. I wanted to be prayer in action. 

Now, as I continue to reflect and process world events and history, I find myself needing prayer again. No action seems like it’s enough in light of so many genocides we have committed, witnessed, and suffered as a collective. 

So I light candles, make offerings and pray. I pray that we will learn from our mistakes so as not to repeat them. I pray for suffering to be meaningful when it does happen. I pray we’ll do better with every passing generation. 

I pray with words spoken and words offered silently in my heart. 

I prayed, I pray and I am praying.

posts.caption:
There are so many celebrations in the month of May! Cinco de Mayo, Mother’s Day, Pentecost, Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month, and the Month of Mother Mary. There’s so much life buzzing throughout the land in May 🪻🦋🐝🐞🐿️

This year in California, there has been so much rain and the land has really come to life. There are so many flowers blooming everywhere—even in the dessert! Just as the land is moving and growing, I feel called to do the same. 

This May, I feel called to preserve old traditions and to create new ones. 

As an Asian American born and raised in California, I had access to a Korean specific grocery store early on in childhood, rather than having to go to the general Asian or Oriental Markets. I had people around me I could speak Korean to, and a tiny local VHS rental shop that had Korean cartoons that I could watch and learn Korean from. Growing up surrounded by Korean in a land an ocean away from where my ancestors had lived, was certainly a blessing and a privilege. 

Being surrounded by all of it, remembering and recording skills I had learned or stories I’d been told were not high on my priority list. 

Now, my grandparents have all passed on, and I realize how significant their traditions have been as I develop my own traditions. 

Here I am today, on a road that no one would have guessed I would take all those years ago. A mudang apprentice learning the old ways and learning new ways. All the clouds and rain from past years have brought me so many flowers that I can enjoy and cherish in my life.

I’m really looking forward to the month of May, and honoring old traditions, as well as, forging my own path and creating new traditions. 

What are you most looking forward to this May?

posts.caption:
I was gifted my first 도장 stamp as a 무당 mudang. I’m grateful for all the people in my life who support me and the path I’ve chosen. Through gifts, their time and energy, words of wisdom, and in other ways, I’m lucky to have people in my corner who accept me and this unconventional life I lead. 

Someone asked me if becoming a mudang had led me to reconnecting to my Korean heritage. I realized it had not, because this need to honor my roots started years ago. I spent my whole life being in the grey areas and the in-between. Neither here nor there, yet still here and there. My heritage is complicated and it’s more than Korean. It’s also Japanese. It’s more than just Seoul (though I speak 서울말 Seoul dialect), it’s 황해도 Hwanghae, 전라도 Jeolla, 경상남도 Gyeongsangnam, 오사카 Osaka. Not to mention I was born and raised in the U.S. 

Becoming a mudang hasn’t led me to reconnecting to my Korean heritage. 

I’m not Korean. I’m not Japanese. I’m not American. Yet, I am all of those things and more. I have my own path to walk that requires me to know who I am and why I am.  Most importantly, I need to forge my own path and continue to grow into who I need to be. 

Becoming a mudang hasn’t led me to reconnecting to my Korean heritage, but it has shown me that I’m not alone. 

It has shown me we don’t always have to walk alone in our respective paths. We need only look up and around us to see that there are many others on their own unique journeys of becoming. There is power in connecting to our roots, and then there is the power of stepping into who we are. They go hand in hand. Everyday as a baby mudang 애동제자, I take steps towards becoming who I am and building my own legacy.

posts.caption:
Transmission from the cave. SAJU: the study of time or Destiny?

I use to think of time as a circle, a cycle; stuck repeating over, and over. But now as a spiral with these lesson meeting me deeper with time.

posts.caption:
We know the sacred lives in the mundane. As digital media consumption expands and Korean shamanism steps onto a global stage, the tradition becomes newly visible. Morphing into something that can be packaged, branded, and consumed.

Applications for trademark THE MUDANG, MUDANG MI or THE BABY MUDANG as a brand or business with NO CLAIM to the exclusive rights of MUDANG doesn not absolve impact of harm.

The question is, what happens if such a mark is granted?


According to the public Notice of Non-Final Office Action filed on 6/5/2026 for the application of THE BABY MUDANG. States an  Advisory regarding Potential Section 2(d) Refusal because of a prior-filed application by THE MUDANG. 

If the trademark for THE MUDANG does get approved, then THE BABY MUDANG gets rejected “because of the likelihood of confusion between the two marks.”

This highlights exactly what I was afraid of. The moment one practitioner's mark is granted, the next one becomes a "likelihood of confusion" to be refused. 

One by one, the tradition's own name becomes something we can be shut out of.

Thank you 
Mudang Jenn 
🙏

posts.caption:
Exactly one year ago today, I was admitted into the hospital. 

7 hours and 3 blood transfusion later, my surgical team removed a 17-20 lbs fibroid that had fused with my inner organs from adenomyosis. Months prior to this, with anemia and blood issues leading to slow organ failure, my body was shutting down. 

This was an accumulation of many things, and in some way - a second kind of spiritual  sickness because I wasn't stepping up to my work. Another kind of shin-byeong, when the knives starts to come into the body. 

After surgery, 3 months later I hit the stage in Pittsburgh for the  Futurity of the Womb, myth of the Cyborg Kiaseng project. A experimental performance art retelling Korean mythology from a feminist perspective with burlesque and demonology. 

And since then,  I haven't looked back, stepping into my work fully now. 
I will probably go write/record a substack on this.

We are going to talk about Shin-byeong in depth.

posts.caption:
Opening on April 18th at Green-Wood’s Main Entrance Meadow, ‘Offering’ is a new installation by artist Jean Shin (@jean.shin). Inspired by Korean burial mounds, the work gathers trunks, branches, and leaves from across the Cemetery into a living memorial that will continue to change over time. ✨🌱

Rather than marking an ending, ‘Offering’ follows a different kind of timeline. As the materials slowly decompose, they enrich the soil beneath and support new growth. In the coming seasons, native wildflowers will take root, drawing pollinators, birds, and other life into the space.

Join us during our grand opening celebration for the Green-House (April 18th & 19th) for Nurturing the Remains: A Community Ritual at Jean Shin’s Offering (3–5pm). The program begins in the Modern Chapel with an introduction by the artist, followed by a community ritual led by Mudang Jenn (@shaman.mudang), and continues with a visit to the Green-House to view Celadon Landscape.

Register at the link in our bio!

—

‘Offering’ is curated by Harry J. Weil (@harryw83), Green-Wood’s Vice President of Education and Public Programs. This installation is made possible by the New York State Council on the Arts, with support from the Office of the Governor and the New York State Legislature.

Celebrate the Lunar New Year with us at Green-Wood 🌕 

Join us on Sunday, February 22nd, from 1–3pm, for “Nurturing the Remains: A Ritual at Jean Shin’s Offering,” a free, participatory in-person program centered on renewal, care, and the cycles that connect life, death, and regrowth. 

Set around ‘Offering,’ a site-specific installation by Jean Shin (@jean.shin) inspired by Korean tumuli burial mounds, this piece honors fallen trees as living ancestors, returning their trunks, branches, and leaves to the soil to nourish what comes next. 

The program begins with reflections from Jean Shin and Gabrielle Gatto (@gabriellegatteaux), followed by a guided ritual led by Mudang Jenn (@shaman.mudang). Together, we’ll take part in reflective writing, gathering branches, and a fire ceremony to mark the Fire Horse year and welcome the approach of spring. 

This program is free and open to all! We just ask that you please register in advance at the link in our bio. 

Offering is curated by Harry J. Weil, Green-Wood’s Vice President of Education and Public Programs. This installation is made possible by the New York State Council on the Arts, with support from the Office of the Governor and the New York State Legislature.

posts.caption:
Gratitude and blessing to the land
I love working in the dirt. Garden recap of 2025. And most importantly growing food that I can eat/share with my family and neighbors. 

In 굿 kut/gut ceremony we share blessings and abundance through offerings and food. Celebration of joy, love and success is meant to be shared and celebrated together. 

I teach my kids what it means to nuture and care, to work our energies towards building sustainability so that our communities thrive. 

Planning my garden, designing and the care it requires to support its growth has been a BIG learnings in maintain relationship to myself, my work, and how it expands to teach us to hold better relationships externally, internally, spiritually and energetically. 

We were born in the dark, but meant to live in the light. If you think about, we are flowers blooming. Your spirits, ancestors and the divine energy from nature and cosmos demands it so.

It was wonderful to take part in a dialogue and share space celebrating Sulwhasoo visions of heritage, beauty, and longevity.

But these flags are not just flags, its carries meaning, story, connection, history and spirits.

He holds the largest collection of candid shots of you, now displayed in your memorial and museums. Your absence is felt deeply. 

We continue to honor you with offerings and gratitude. Thank you, Corky, your legacy that still breathes through every frame of Peter's work.

posts.caption:
For our September Town Hall, A4 gathers artists whose work preserves cultural traditions and ancestral knowledge.⁠
⁠
Featured presenters include @shaman.mudang, a diaspora shaman, ritual performance artist, and teacher, who will discuss her experience bringing an ancient Korean folk religion to present-day audiences. We’ll also hear from @sabri, a Palestinian American painter and textile artist, who will present about his tatreez practice and his approach to community engagement.⁠
⁠
Additionally, the evening will feature a line-up of brief pitches from the community. After the presentations, we’ll host a potluck meal, so please bring something to share; homemade or store bought items are welcome. A4 will provide drinks.⁠
⁠
For those who would like to continue mingling after the event, we recommend The Binc or Henry St. Ale House near the venue.⁠
⁠
🎟️ This event is FREE and open to the public. We suggest a $5 donation to go towards keeping A4’s programs free. RSVP is required to attend and/or pitch, but you do not have to pitch to attend. #linkinbio⁠
⁠
📍@asiaartarchiveinamerica⁠
📆 9/25, 6:30–8:30pm⁠
⁠
#asiaartarchive #a4

✨Futurity of the Womb: Myth of the Cyborg Kisaeng is a 60-minute performance reimagining Korean history through feminist cosmology. posts.caption:
Initiation - I dont take that shit lightly. And so many people get angry and upset with me because my views are strong about initiation. 

The fact I have to even come on here to explain why initiation is very sacred and important. 

Straight up, I have lost people who died from bad initiation and kut ceremony. And know too many people who got severely injured or hurt AFTER the initiation. Car accidents  are very common happenings that I see as a result of improper kut ceremonies. It's because of this that I struggle with ceremony, and I dont take it lightly at all. 

The process,  the process, the ceremony process!!!! The process of initiation is the MOST IMPORTANT. Stop watering down the fucking process. 

Some people their energy is way too sensitive and fucked just to have anyone touch you. Like honestly, would any of you go get surgery from someone who doesn't even specialize or trained? 

I've only done initiations and other ceremonies since I stepped into this practice. But even I wont fuck around with this, and will approach with care AND caution. Please, for the love of God, try sitting in a ceremony first before initiating. 

Let the mass unfollowing begin. Because I wont say the things you want to hear. 

You dont need to initiate to have a spiritual practice. You dont initiate to build a relationship. 
#initiation #closedpractice  #shamanism
