comments.text: What I think about this is that social media and other media exploits only the positive part in everything but rare show the negative side to it. Which is people not researching enough about people traditional culture. Some things are just not for you because of aspects of certain things. But they ignore it and that when real trouble begins.

THIS is 100% correct. I've heard the same complaints over in the Haitian side, and YES, you can't initiate someone after they only saw only ONE ceremony or "a few" (or haven't had other ritual experience in the culture before advancing into initiation). Sad part with Mugyo is that many Koreans are reluctant to even attend a kut or shin ceremony of some kind, and you get the stories of some manshin basically running an initiation mill for certain desperate folks (same story here in the US with certain corrupt practitioners in Cuban Ocha and Haitian Vodou where they not only immediately initiate and take money from their godkids, but then refuse to teach them anything instead of developing a relation of many years). As they say, not everyone is destined to initiate (and some folks simply weren't meant be involved in this practice in the first place)
무식하면 용감하다 is the phrase that comes to mind! There's so much ignorance and romanticization around initiation. People forget or ignore the danger.

THIS people want the title without taking the necessary steps. It just shows that they don’t take spirituality seriously. A doctor who bought their degree from a back alley is in NO WAY qualified unlike a doctor who went to school, completed their residency, and formed a foundation for their practice.
Wow… definitely energies that shouldn’t be messed with (in the wrong way), never thought of it in terms of shaman initiations. That’s mental that you know people who have died from this 😮
Truth!!!!!!!!!! I'm sorry that you experienced loss. Thank you for sharing this vital information.

Need to clarify that I dont reject people from exploring. I will happily encourage it, its so much more powerful and sustainable  when ot is personal to you, your stories, and ancestors. There more than one path up the mountain, and in some cases, we have to make our path.  But I would push back and hold on initiations (personal opinion) because why wait to build that connection. Start now, start today. You dont need initiation ceremony,  you need to listen to you, heart and spirits. Let it take you on your journey and help navigate. Initiation ceremonies are called 내림 meaning descent, to come down. In truth I prefer 신굿 or calling it 내림. Because what are we bringing down, in truth it was always within us. 🔥

⌛️7:30-8:30PM
✨Alloy Studios - @kstheater 

📍Purchase tickets in our bios! 

✨𝑭𝒖𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒊𝒕𝒚 𝒐𝒇 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝑾𝒐𝒎𝒃: 𝑴𝒚𝒕𝒉 𝒐𝒇 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝑪𝒚𝒃𝒐𝒓𝒈 𝑲𝒊𝒔𝒂𝒆𝒏𝒈 is an experimental, 60-minute multimedia performance reimagining Korean history through the lens of feminist mythology. Blending ritual, burlesque, speculative fiction, and mythology, the piece unfolds in four sections interweaving live performance, video projection, and audience interaction.

✨Traditionally, kisaengs were enslaved Korean courtesans, forced to entertain those in power while mastering the arts. Futurity of the Womb is a time-traveling performance that redefines the kisaeng’s legacy beyond the constraints of history. The cyborg becomes a vessel for interrogating our  codependence with technology and identity, reflecting on power manufactured by human limitations. 

🌌Mudang Jenn Kim, a Korean-American shaman, invokes the first cosmic mother of Korea, MAGO,  who was shamed for her larger-than-life power. 

🪄Kayla Tange, merges the kisaeng and abandoned Princess Bari to explore grief and adoption as a portal—dwelling in the space between the living and the dead.

🩸C. Ryu reimagines the gumiho, a nine-tailed fox demon that consumed men’s livers and hearts to survive, as a cyborg— alchemizing complicit desire.

✨Futurity of the Womb offers not a single narrative, but a timeline rewritten—a mythos where stories once censored emerge alive, electric, and here. This is not a return to history—it’s a reprogramming.

✨✨Funding for the “Futurity of the Womb: Myth of the Cyborg Kisaeng” was provided by the Exposure Artists Program of @the_pittsburgh_foundation , An additional thank you for the support provided by the Pedantic Arts Residency.

세월이 지나고 거의 10년이 다 왔네요.
10년이 다 와도 저는 애동 제자라고 아직도 생각합니다.
10년이든 20년이든 30년이든 신의 길이 가게 되면 배울 거가 너무 많아요.

사람마다 그릇이 다르죠.
법당에 매달리면서 기도하면서 저는 어떤 그릇이 될까?
한국 글을 쓰는게 아직도 불편해서 잘 못 해요.

I use to work 굿 kut ceremonies alot (w/ elder), sometimes 3x a week for years. Our bodies were pushed to extreme with little sleep, navigating all the energies of the clients and their spirits while navigating our own personal lives. 

Sometimes, I didn't have time to breathe or have energy to take care of my own family because I was laid out after 굿 ceremony. 

굿 kut/gut takes alot of energy, needs lots of support, and hands involved to bring the ceremonies together.  We cannot perform 굿 kut/gut ceremonies alone. 

My path and training as mudang is very traditional. I shadowed my elder teacher every single day for YEARS. Way beyond the technical 3 years of basic training. 

I have given myself fully to this path. 
And that also has cause alot of pain within myself

another project will soon will be coming. 

*** I did not translate the Korean words into English. Some words have to be said and expressed in Korean to fully express the depth I feel.

posts.caption:
Its time to re-introduce myself. 

Life brought me inward these past few months, deeper into my own body, my own healing, my own truth. After surgery and a forced slowdown, I’ve been tending to what doesn’t get seen: grief, rest, recovery, and remembrance. 

I’m Mudang Jenn, my Korean shaman name is 신수 보살 Sinsu Bosal - initiated in 2016. A Korean shaman, ritual artist, and spiritual teacher walking with those reclaiming ancestral ways where spirit is not just spoken of, but felt, moved, and remembered in the body. I help people remember what was never really lost: spirit, intuition, and the power of devotion. it’s ancestral duty and ancestor in training in real time. 

I hold private sessions, offer handmade spiritual items and ritual candles, and teach the old ways so they can live through us now. not as folklore but as living, breathing and flowing practice. 

 I’m a Leo Sun, Cancer Moon, Scorpio Rising. So yes, I’ll hold your hand through the underworld and remind you you’re not alone.
In eastern astrology, zodiac sign of rat, an energy tied to fluidity, neither yang nor yin but in between this world and the spirit world. 

My calendar will slowly reopen for sessions as I return to work with care and intention at the end of this month. I’m keeping things paced. Focused. Aligned. There are new offerings in the works, crafted in prayer and ritual. If you’ve been in a transformation of your own, in the quiet, unseen....I feel you. 

We’re still walking. Still remembering. Still rising. 

**an old picture from 내림 신굿 2016

Today is Samjitnal, 삼짇날 the celebration of Spring's renewing energy, blooming with life. The plants are stirring slowly poking through the ground, and the swallows have returned. 

Today also happens to be my first day back after a two month retreat.  I had to step away, I needed it. That's when the drums started to sound, calling me.

Slowed down and rested.

Thank you for being here. 
So much to share, 
so much is flowing and pouring.

But today, I honor the first bloom. 
The season of return
back home 
to you. 

With love and drum beats, 
💛 Jenn 무당젠

posts.caption:
Part of an annually released mini-documentary series that paints vivid, visual stories of unique Korean Americans and their passions for their craft, NAYA (나야): Shaman Mudang dives into the journey of Jennifer Kim, a practitioner of musok from New York.

As she processes her own childhood traumas and experiences, Mudang Jenn shares a story of the spiritual challenges which propelled her towards working on her relationships with family, as well as the active choice to meaningfully work towards healing within her communities. Cultivating tradition to respond to contemporary anxieties, she focuses her talents and calling to address the han latent throughout the Korean diaspora.

Watch the full documentary on our YouTube channel, link in bio🔗

posts.caption:
I’ve received so many messages and comments about Player 044 Seon-nyeo and the depiction of mudangs (shaman) in Squid Game Season 2. I have to say, I absolutely hated how it was portrayed. It perpetuates harmful stigmas surrounding the indigenous spiritual practices of our ancestors, continuing a cycle of misunderstanding and disrespect. From Confucian scholars to the Japanese Occupation to the modernization movement in Korea, these negative stigmans have created harmful narratives for centuries. 

Recently, I was approached by a team working on an official Squid Game podcast hosted by a prominent Korean American content creator. They invited me to share insights about Korean shamanism in relation to the series. Initially, I was hopeful about the opportunity to educate and shed light on our traditions. I spent time answering their questions, engaging in meaningful conversations, and offering my expertise.

Unfortunately, my experience quickly turned sour. Not only did they fail to honor anything we discussed, but they also disrespected me by not crediting my work, time, or labor. In today’s age, it’s standard practice to tag or credit collaborators—this is the bare minimum. Instead, when I raised these concerns, it was escalated to someone higher up who attempted to "resolve" the issue by offering me money to stay quiet and complacent.

This behavior is unacceptable. When we collaborate within our communities, respect must be the foundation. Experiences like this are why I’ve decided that I will no longer work with large creators or media productions without clear, formal agreements in place from the get. 

Respect and accountability matter, especially when representing marginalized and sacred practices.

#mudang #koreanshamanism #mudangjenn #squidgameseason2 #asianamerican

posts.caption:
I’ve always struggled with being seen. If it were up to me, I’d be tucked away in the mountains, living a reclusive life. Growing up, even something as simple as lining up for lunch at school, felt impossible—the fear of drawing attention was paralyzing.

But as I got older, I began to confront that fear. You can see the change within my IG feed, went from hiding to showing myself more. I’ve worked hard to embrace taking up space and being seen. It hasn’t been easy, but I’ve learned to stand in my truth, even when it feels uncomfortable.

With the rise of interest in Korean culture and heritage, there’s a growing curiosity about Korean shamanism. And while it’s exciting to see this our practices and tradition acknowledged, it also brings challenges. Big companies and media producers are taking notice, and unfortunately, that doesn’t always come with the respect or credit these traditions—and the people carrying them—deserve.

I’ve had to fight for recognition for my contributions. I had to stand up to Apple TV during their Pachinko series for proper acknowledgment, and now, I’m facing another battle with a major Korean-American content creator and media platform.

Lol. I went from fearing visibility to having to demand to be seen, heard, and credited. It’s not just about me—it’s about respecting the cultural traditions I represent and the labor, energy, and spirit that go into this work.

If you’re reading this, thank you for seeing me. And thank you for helping me take up space.

⭐️It’s okay to feel uncomfortable with being seen, but remember—you have a voice, a story, and a presence that matters. You are worthy of being seen and heard. Progress doesn’t happen overnight, so celebrate the small wins—whether it’s speaking up, sharing your truth, or holding your ground. Each step forward is growth.

#koreanshaman #koreanshamanism #mudangjenn #kdrama #koreanamerican #koreandiaspora #squidgames #takeupspace

posts.caption:
The Cholera cat was a bujeok that was pasted on the front door of homes to ward off the sickness of the rat. People believe cholera came from the demon spirit of the rat - so naturally the cat became a protector. 

During a cholera outbreak in Korea, the perception of cats shifted dramatically. Historically, cats were often viewed as fey or even vile creatures, but during the cholera epidemic—known as 쥐통 (literally "rat pain/sickness")—they became protectors against disease.

The connection? Rats were seen as carriers of sickness, and cats, as natural predators of rats, symbolized protection. This gave rise to cat bujeoks, protective talismans featuring cats, which I find absolutely adorable!

Interestingly, in folk magic, rats hold dual symbolism. In some practices, they are seen as bringers of fortune and blessings, while in others, they represent misfortune and chaos. This complex relationship reflects the nuanced ways animals are perceived in folk practices 

The government even employed firecrackers and gunfire, believing the noise would scare away disease spirits. This fascinating blend of spiritual beliefs and practical solutions reflects the rich layers of Korean folk traditions.

Maybe I will write more about this on my blog - Mudang Life to explain further sharing resources. 

When I use to have alot of spiritual hauntings - my cats were there to alert and protect me. I'm more of a cat person than a dog person - I wouldn't mind a colony of cats loafing around but my family and kids are severely allergic. 🫠

#koreanfolkmagic #koreanshamanism #shamanism #folkmagic #bujeok #amulets #talisman #cat #wardoffevil #protectorspirits #spirituality

posts.caption:
Tried Yemeni coffee for the first time at @qahwah_house! My partner ordered for me,  the Mofawar coffee with cardamom and cream—absolutely delicious. The cardamom adds a floral, earthy warmth that’s so comforting. I’m curiously happy to support this newly opened Middle Eastern coffee shop in my neighborhood.

Growing up in Queens, cultural diversity was a huge part of my life. My old neighborhood near 77th Road and Parsons Blvd was a true melting pot. We had the Pomonok projects, the Electchester union community, and a vibrant Middle Eastern community where the mosque’s prayers echoed beautifully through loudspeakers. There was also a strong Jewish community and Kosher pizzerias, and then there was me—one of the few East Asians in the mix. That environment shaped me, and I love seeing spaces like this coffee shop bring that same rich diversity to life.

#yemenicoffee #supportlocalbusiness
#culturaldiversity #childhoodmemories #meltingpot #coffee

I harvested these sweet potatoes that were planted earlier, and seeing them covered in roots is beautiful. Growing in the dark, beneath the soil, they’ve absorbed the nutrients and energy of the earth’s womb.

It made me reflect on our own beginnings. There's a saying that we are born alone, but I see it differently. 

Like these sweet potatoes, tangled with roots, we come into this world deeply connected—attached by the placenta, grounded and nurtured even before we take our first breath.

Watered by the guardian spirits and ancestors, we are nourished and shaped within the womb. Just as the sweet potatoes draw life from the soil, we too are sustained by the unseen hands of those who came before us, growing strong and rooted in the sacred bonds that connect us to the past.

posts.caption:
Didn't take any proper Chuseok photos of offerings, so much chaos. 

I'm grateful for the safety of my children and family. The last two days, FBI and Homeland Security, was called to my kids' school for threats of violence. It prompted the school to go into lockdown. It brought out so much worry and anxiety as a parent and mother. 

I am grateful that our school and community acted quickly to make sure our kids are safe. But this is ridiculous, I will never forget the time when my 1st grader came home to tell me about his lockdown drill in case a bad person comes in. 

Our system is fucked and backwards. Police will patrol subway stations and will shoot pedestrians over 2.90 fare causing more harm and menance. People will fight hard for their right to bear arms or gun safety but won't bring the same energy to protect our youth and children. How is a piece of metal and steel triumph the lives of our kids, children, and community. 

This Chuseok, we are supposed to give thanks, gratitude and celebrate. I give thanks that my children and family is safe and also pray yours is too. 

#chuseok #midautumnfestival #fullmoon

posts.caption:
Having good harvest from your garden = being blessed by the spirits. In our practices and traditions, having a bountiful garden means the spirits will bless you with abundance. My elder once told me that based on how things "grow" in the garden equate to success, blessings and abundance from the spirits. 

Our shamanic practices and celebration revolved about the farming practices of our ancestors.  When we have a good harvest, we celebrate and make offerings to the spirits and deities. 

Our gods and deities are often spirits of nature, protectors and guardians of the natural world. Sanshin 산신, god and protector of mountains. Yongwang 용왕, god of rain, water, and oceans. Jishin 지신, the spirit of the earth. All the spirits within the pantheon of our shamanism is the spirits and protectors of nature. 

How do you interact with the earth and nature? 
How do you connect with the spirits? 

Simply connecting with nature around you is interacting with the gods/deities of our shamanic world. 

#guardians #deities #gods #animism #shamanism #koreanspirituality #koreanshaman #mudangjenn #shamanmudang #muism #mugyo #abundance

posts.caption:
I've never used to like flowers, but lately been feeling so much joy hovering over flowers. I go out to the yard everyday to watch and look at the flowers growing. It's such a surprise to see what they bloom into. 

Flowers and plants absorb the yang energy of the sun. In spiritual practices that involve cleansing, purification, and exorcism , it's a battle of energies. We bring yang energies using plants and flowers to "battle" the yin energies of negativity, pollution, and attachments. 

Flowers play a significant role in our shamanic practices. Artificial flowers made of paper, silk, and other materials are used on our altars for spirits to sit upon the petals. We avoid flowers or plants with thorns, as they can repel spirits, unless specifically used to ward off negativity and attachments. During ceremonies, when we call in the souls and spirits of our ancestors, they are gently cared for as they sit upon the petals.

Lately there's been such heavy energies - sitting, processing and going with the flow. Next month is in the energy of horse month. Ohhh how fun for those with rat in their chart, a clashing energy. 

#koreanshamanism #iris #mudangjenn #koreanspirituality
#folkmagic #spiritualpractice #easternastrology #saju #cleansing #flowermagic #musok #mugyo #muism #zodiac #yangenergy #yinenergy

Drove into the city in K-town for a quick minute, crossing over the 59th, stopped by my old stomping grounds of Astoria, Queens. You know I had to pick up some Palestinian street food at Freddy's. 

20 years ago, as a student at Hunter CUNY I would always stop by Freddy's food cart by the Ctown parking lot. He had the biggest smile, always great conversation  and best food. His food and love were always so comforting. I always try to stop by and support whenever I get a chance to. 

20 years later, I still feel the love and care whenever I have his food. The best ever. 

#kingoffalafel #Astoria #palestinianstreetfood #nostalgia

posts.caption:
Remembering my partners grandmother, the ancestor to my children - Yang Yi. Her life story lives on with our family. We lost her due to Covid complications at 103. 

Our children will learn about grandma's love for literature, writing, and art. How she fought against Japanese imperialism and occupation operating an underground newspaper for the people. 

My partners childhood home belonging to his grandmother, now turned into a museum. One day we hope to bring our children to grandma's museum home to learn about the stories of their great-grandmother. 

It's different for my side of the family, especially when I don't know the stories. Memories was too painful for my grandmother, she never shared about her life, family or how she lived. She crossed over from North Korea on her own during the Korean War. Settling in Paju, operating a rice farm and supply store in hopes to reunite with her family - but never did. 😭

May the stories of our ancestors continue to be told and not forgotten. 

#ancestors #aapi #aanhpi #storytelling #ancestorhealing #yangyi #杨静如 #杨苡

posts.caption:
Candy offerings for my child spirits Dongja & Dongyeo 동자 동녀. 
Working with child spirits can be fickle, especially if they are upfront and active. Child spirits have different duties depending on their "role(s)" within the pantheon. 

The most common role of child spirits is to assist the other spirits by running errands, or helping out. Child spirits are also capable of doing divination depending on their intuition and abilities. Children can get easily upset. They want to be nurtured and cared for.  I make sure to plant golden yellow flowers (favorite color) , and give lots of candy and thoughtful gifts, including new hanboks and shoes. 

Working with child spirits has been healing for my inner child. We are taught how important children spirits are, as they provide support for the entire pantheon of grandmother and grandfather spirits. Bringing more play into our spiritual practices is a necessary vehicle that allows expression and release. 

The offerings for my child spirits are candy, sweets, chocolate, and toys. Favorite color is yellow or golden, and they love bunnies and ducklings. 🐇🐥 Easter candies are the best with all the duck and bunnies.

#play #mudang #mudangjenn #childspirit #koreanshamanism  #mudang #musok ##mugyo ##altarofferings

posts.caption:
Reposted @koreanamericanstory 

Continuing their special series on cultural topics, Catherine and Juliana discuss the ways Korean Americans are observing age-old traditions like Paebek (wedding tea ceremony), Dol (first birthday) and Jesa (ancestor veneration). Their first guest is event planner Christine Chang of Live Love Create in Los Angeles, who explains how her wedding and Dol clients are honoring their heritage in a “fusion” style that feels relevant to them. (Think: a shorter, more inclusive Paebek or a golf ball included in the doljabi.) Next, they chat with mother-daughter duo Laura Park and Estella Riahi of Leehwa Wedding & Hanbok, a sought-after hanbok studio where LA’s Korean community have been ordering custom garments since the early 1990s. Catherine and Juliana learn how hanbok styles have evolved and how Leewha has become the go-to source for celebs looking for hanboks for awards season. Finally, the hosts speak with Jennifer Kim, aka Mudang Jenn, a shaman based in New York who explains the tradition of Jesa and how Korean Americans are adapting the ritual for today.

posts.caption:
MY UNPOPULAR MUDANG OPINION: Altars and offerings as display of wealth. 

We are taught to use the best products, premium items for our altars and offerings. Korean mudangs teach that having a grand altar with overly flowing offerings is the "proper" way of expressing gratitude. Similarly, how traditional jesa 세사 ancestral altars are flowing abundantly with food and offerings. 

These grand altars with overflowing food and offerings are displays of wealth. Our traditional practices often follow the practices of the elite and ruling aristocratic social class. I cannot help but feel these ceremonies and practice mimics the grandiose displays by royalty or elite. Or whenever we speak on traditions, it's often centered on practices of Hanyang (Seoul) of Joseon Dynasty. 

It's why these ceremonies cant be accessible by everyone. Its specifically taught to me by my elder, that "everyone does not have the right or privilege to 굿 ceremony." So, does that mean poor folks or those in need have no right to healing, storytelling or agency? That started my radical journey of inquiries, questioning, and criticism. 

Automatically, our shamanic practices exclude the very people that our spaces, ceremonies, and rituals were originally meant for - those marginalized within our communities. Our shamanic traditions were meant to uplift the people, not the elite and wealthy. 
 

Side note: If you have been following me, you will notice my content has shifted in sharing about our shamanic practices and traditions. On my journey to reconnecting with traditions of Korea, I've also experienced alot of difficulties learning and embracing our practices. This is sharing my journey of learning and unlearning meant to plant seeds of inquiries within us. 

Its my personal belief that our shamanic practices are meant to uplift and empower us. All of us, power to the people. 

⬇️⬇️⬇️ See comments for more info/context of photos. 

#koreanshamanism #shamanism #shaman #mudangjenn #musok #mugyo #muism #sacredritual #sacredaltar #altar #offerings #shamaniccereminy #kut #koreanspirituality #closedpractice #capitalism #spirituality

posts.caption:
Happy DaeBoreum - the celebrations of the first full moon in the year of the wood blue Dragon. There are so many ways to celebrate the Grand Full Moon. Crafting and burning a moon house, or daljip, a communal practice that involves, ritual fire with sending your wishes, prayers and petitions to the moon and the heavens. 

Fire, a sacred element brings in energies of transmutation, the transformational change ignited by ceremonial fire. The prayers, desires, and petitions are inscribed on white paper and cast into the flames as the moon house is lit. This act symbolizes the transformation of written words into ashes, which are then carried by the wind to the heavens. Similar to the Phoenix bird, being reborn and rising from the ashes. 

The year of the Dragon brings in energy of power, change, and transformation. 

May we all rise from the ashes
In power with one another.

posts.caption:
Almost 5am, couldn't sleep because I was cold and couldn't warm up. My most FAVORITE thing in the world is soaking in hot water, in the dark with a nightlight on. The peace and quietness, as everyone sleeps and I'm just soaking, charging and relaxing. 

A reminder to myself I am not a young spring chicken anymore as I'm approaching 40 😊. My Chinese doctor will scold me if he found out I've been munching on ice cubes as a snack -  my doctor Sam will yell at me, no cold food or drinks. 

I hope to make space for myself more this year. Listen to my body and energy levels - cause Im coming down with a cold. I didn't realize how much I was pushing through this week - hard making space without emptying first, there's no room. 

Something I read that's stayed with me - if you don't set healthy boundaries, your body will. As someone autoimmune and Ehlers Danlos (waiting for diagnosis and confirmation) - this hits home. 

In ceremonial spaces and earlier teachings of my elder - we are taught to be the sacrificial lamb. That we must put our bodies first, that it's noble and honorable when you sacrifice your time, energy, bodies, health, etc. The same narrative in our capitalist society. During Covid, when there was mandatory lockdowns, my elder still held ceremonies, completing ignoring the risks and warnings. It was all for money, because if you give clients time to think - they will change their minds about ceremony. Its why we often rush into ceremony preparations. 

I was their laborer, personal assistant, and many things. I wasn't allowed to form my own opinions or thoughts - only allowed to do as I have been told or instructed, and the gaslighting is insane. Especially in circumstances when I had to choose between my family and my elders' money-making ceremonies. 

They say they love you, respect you, and call you family. While talking about you, belittling you and looking down on you. All manipulation and grooming tactics. Energy doesnt lie, I struggled with this for years in the spirit house/family - last year, I finally said no. I cut ties and burned bridges with the spirit family, including my toxic spirit siblings. 

Left and never looked back. 
Liberated.

At my local cafe in a meeting, chatting with a researcher. Sharing about my life's experiences, childhood,  family, and my journey as a diaspora Korean shaman mudang. I've been so proud of this path, the honor to walk with ancestors and held by the spirits. 

But when the interviewer asked me, "What is the best thing about being a mudang". 

Instantly my face changed, and strong emotions flooded into my body. I was so shocked by this strong emotional response, I didn't know what to with it but break down and cry. 
I was so embarrassed at my unexpected behavior. Yet a powerful emotion, a learning moment. 

So much grief doing this work, and walking this path. I dont think its something people realized, including myself. Didn't realize how much my body was holding until I was asked this question. Took some deep breath, wiped away streaming tears, and regained my composure. 

The first thing to fly out of my mouth in response was nothing. I don't know, I don't know. 
If I really could, I wouldn't choose this path or journey. 

But in truth, walking this path push me to expand further than what I thought. Expanding my capacity,  breaking down everything to make room and space for more.

posts.caption:
동지 Dongji house cleansing ritual to clear the homes, personal spaces, and businesses. 

Corean pat red beans are used specifically for cleansing and exorcism. The color red chases away negativity, pollution, and clears spaces - stemmed from mythology story of Gongongshi. Whose son died on Winter Solstice becoming the spirit of plague, patjuk was cooked to ward off his spirit and influence. 

Patjuk was put up as offerings in every space outside and within the home. A reminder that working with the energies of our house spirits is important, AND additionally working with the land/earth spirits where your space resides. 

During Winter Solstice, there are many rituals to cleanse the home, business, and personal spaces. This is a reminder that our bodies are also sacred altars. What are some weight and heaviness that you carry within you that you are ready to release and let go of?

And yes, Winter edition of Musok Life is out. Sorry for the long delay and a huge shoutout to Wonhee for their magic, helping me with it.

Some rituals and ceremonies require purification of the body and must abstain from sex, meat, and liquor. For modern practices, I would also include abstaining from cannabis. And yet, somehow cigarettes are okay. 

Back when I was initiating, my elder made sure I did not consume any meat or eggs - just purely vegan. The ceremony spaces then had workers who prepared meals and helped  out - they would never serve things like eggs. 

Now, you can see many changes and shifts to our practices. Even Buddhist temples serves kimchi for their morning breakfast back then anything spicy with chilli, garlic, onions and scallions were avoided. In recent years, even my elder forgo restrictions meant for body purification. 

Things back then, even just 5 years ago were much stricter. 

In this video, prepping for client ritual for multiple nights. Each night, the food and fruit offerings are taken down - refreshed with new fruits and cooked offerings. This is second night, refreshing the fruits on the ancestor altar.

posts.caption:
무당 Mudangs = chosen by god. 
Within traditional shaman cultures, the narrative is the same across. You must be chosen by the gods, deities, the spirits. I find alot of this narrative to be extremely problematic for many reasons. 

What does it mean? Who are the gods? 

It's been a blessing to be on this path as a mudang, a Korean shaman. When I accepted this calling, it was lonely. There was no one around me to discuss or share the experiences and difficulties - even in my own spirit family lineage because no one else was working as a mudang. 

Alot of people don't know that being chosen or initiated doesn't mean you are a mudang or a spirit worker. In fact, many people initiate with intentions of never practicing as a shaman.

Does shinbyung (shamanic sickness) equate to mudang? In my experience, the answer is no. There's various types of spirit affliction and influences. 

Did you know, initiation is big money-making for Korean shamans. It can cost upwards of 20k or more - personally in my own journey, I've spent over 100k in ceremonies alone. Of course there is no such thing as free labor. 

I've gotten so many messages from people interested in initiations and from those who have initiated but have no guidance on their paths from their elders. 

Let's talk about it 
Ready to unpack the purpose of initiation, the history of ceremonies, the training involved, and everything that's unique to the paths of us, Korean diaspora. 

I've been walking this path for over 7 years officially, and majority of my experience has been opening doors and paths for others. 

Will be announcing dates for discussion, chats and Q&As. A critical and deeper look into our traditions. Will possibly turn this into monthly chats and discussions - open to everyone. 

Please subscribe to my newsletter on my website for announcements. I switched over to another platform and did not transfer my contacts. Will be sending out more information on these chats and discussions. 

Free and open to all for discussion. 

#koreanshaman #mudangjenn #koreanshamanism #closedpractices #koreanspirituality #musok #mugyo #initiation #naerimkut #gods #deities #spirits #ancestors #spiritworker #koreandiaspora

posts.caption:
Last night, I dreamed of a leopard. 

I was in my garden, and I saw that a pumpkin vine had snagged on something. I pulled the vine, like a rope - pulling, and then at the end was a leopard. I was so startled that I ran into my house. 

It tried to enter the home but I shut the door. 
Then it tried to open my windows, and I locked it shut. The leopard tried every window and crevice to enter - and somehow it entered through the second floor window. 

I screamed and hollered. 
Then the leopard spoke and said I am here. 

Woke up pondering what this dream meant. 
For me, dream work is super important - many of my dreams contain wisdom, lessons and messages from my spirits. 

According to online, Leopards can represent a period of rebirth after radical change, healer of deep wounds. Bringing issues to old resolution through reclaiming of your lost power during wounding. This truly resonates with my current life.

I've written this before and Korea was known as the land of leopards. On my red spirit regalia for my mountain spirits, I have leopard on my back. 
Leopards were hunted to extinction during the Japanese Occupation and was referred to the Korean leopard 🐆. 

Ever since I realigned back home to myself, my dreams has been 🔥🔥🔥

What is 인연 destiny? 
A golden thread weaving us together, for however long or short - a connected destiny. 

This Halloween coming up is my initiation anniversary of walking this path as initiated Mudang. And so much had changed, shifted, and evolved - like with everything in nature. 

Connecting with elders is hard. It took me a long time to even find one. It was important for me to meet with elders and people that I can respect and learn from. But my path and spirits lead me otherwise, grown a lot through unexpected ways. 

Truth is, I was out of alignment. I was faced with the harsh truth that the people closest to me were those who I did not align with. My spirit couldn't allow me to continue, and so I left.  Ended many relationships and cut ties. I couldn't take the brewing distrust, racism, capitalist greed, and harmful discrimination towards the trans/queer community anymore. Realizing how damaging it was to my spirit but, importantly, the communities that I care for and love. 

It's feels good.
Coming back to myself. 
Back in alignment 
Back home

And one day, I'm gonna talk about it. 

#communities #alignment #destiny #empowerment #ihatehashtags

From the river to the sea. 
Palestine will be free. 

Kufiya aka Shemagh traditionally worn by farmers, has become the symbol of Palestine freedom and liberation. 
Please do not purchase the Kufiya from Amazon or other sellers profiting from this. Purchase directly from the only Palestinian factory in Palestine Kufiya.org the Hirbawi Kufiya. 

From the factory website: Although Hirbawi founder Yasser Hirbawi passed away in 2018, his three sons carry on the determination, passion, and commitment their father instilled in them, the business, and Palestinian supporters worldwide.⁠ The Hirbawi factory is one of many Palestinian Businesses committed in the struggle to build better lives, and preserve the soul of their ancestors.⁠

To the world, the kufiya will forever be a symbol of liberty. Those who wear it express their desire to see all people, across the world, live peacefully and with self-determination.

The Hirbawi Factory continues its struggle to keep the factory going. In the words of Yasser Hirbawi, “We will continue. This is the fruit of 50 years of continuous work – it’s more than a business. We will remain competitive by continuing to produce the best quality Kufiya”

posts.caption:
HAPPY CHUSEOK!! 🌕🍂[Part 4]

We met with Mudang Jenn @shaman.mudang, a Korean Mudang, who guides us through Chuseok’s history and traditions. Together, let’s explore the cultural significance of our yearly celebration.

Chuseok (추석), also known as Hangawi (한가위) is a centuries-old harvest festival celebrated in both Koreas and within the larger Korean diaspora. It is observed on the 15th day of the 8th month of the lunar calendar (typically between late September/early October) and is closely related to other mid-autumn festivals celebrated by cultures that mark the end of the harvest season. The holiday has roots in Korea’s agrarian customs of old, but continues to serve as a reminder today for us to venerate our connection to nature, spirits, and our ancestors.

A major national holiday in Korea—akin to Thanksgiving in North America—families from all over the country gather to share food, visit ancestral villages, and for some, carry out ancestral rites known as Jesa. Elaborate ritual food and drink are prepared as offerings for the departed, and prayers are delivered to maintain connections between the past and present. Not a religious event, Chuseok emphasizes gratitude for the harvest and reverence for our families. It remains a cherished tradition for Koreans around the globe, uniting them with the generations who came before.

Producer & Editor: @kimberlyyoungsun
DPs: @ajyval & @janicekaramchung

posts.caption:
Headed to NJ for a house ritual yesterday ✨️
House cleansing and protection. 
Weather was beautiful 

Right before leaving, I started to feel sick and nauseous. We call this jigi 지기, when you start to feel the energies of the client and their spirits. It can affect your mood, and change how your body feels. 

We went out to their backyard, hugging the cliffside overlooking the Hudson River. While cleansing, I felt my inside twist, turn and flipped - which is expressed as "internal 5 organs flipping over" 오장육부가 뒤집어진다. 

The gathering of pollution and negative energies gets processed through my body. The energies can be intense, and then a spiritual battle to expel it. Knives come out and gets thrown onto the ground. 
By then my eyes are tearing, nose is dripping, coughing up mucous, gagging and throwing up - expelling. It's never pretty. Takes alot of energy and strength to process. 

There are moments when I pause to think. Can I process this? Taking in the energies to filter through  my own body/energy. Sometimes, those energies we take into us never leaves, and a part of our own energies never returns back to us. 

After this, I went down for a nap but ended up passed out for 2 hours. Much needed rest and care.

posts.caption:
39 years old. 
Birthdays didn't hold alot of meaning for me, it  made me uncomfortable, and tried to downplay as another ordinary day. 

As I get older, I learned to celebrate more. This year I spent my birthday sharing my story, the best gift I can ask for. 

In our Korean culture,  numbers holds energy. When you enter an age ending with 9, you must be cautious because 9 can represent endings. Some people lessened the blow of the 9 number by getting talisman, rituals or ceremonies.  And then there are others who thrive and transform. 

Ending of something doesn't always equate to death and gloom. It can also mean you're shedding weight to make space for more - transformation. 

#birthday #solarreturn #leoseason♌️ #leoseason #numerology #koreanshaman #mudangjenn #shamanmudang #birthday #energy #koreanamerican #asianamerican #scorpiorising

Praying for the protection of our little ones, may the spirits continue to protect our children - carriers of our future, hope. 

Chilseok Day is known as Valentines Day, the mythology of two star-crossed lovers separated by the Milky way galaxy. For mudangs and other Korean shamans, it holds a different significance. Praying to the sky, the heavens and deity guardians has always been part of our ancestral practices.

posts.caption:
Been in discussion in many circles about community, gatherings, and spaces. 

When my parents moved into the mountains, my mom kept having dreams of altars and shrines in the house. Another dream of a white glowing pig walking down the mountain path and 5 colored flags on the rooftops. 

Taking it as a sign, I've been looking for space but maybe it's been there all along - I didn't have to look outside. 

Slowly making plans to create space at my parents' mountain home for talks, gatherings, community, and possible ritual and ceremonies. We can learn about some mountain forage food and local ingredients using my mom's (family) recipes. Most likely will be next year.

August is Leo season 🦁Rawr. 
It's also my birthday month. 🎂

posts.caption:
How powerful and electrifying it is to be with so many Korean diaspora and friends from all over to gather and fight for peace. A call to end the 70th year armistice of Korea. When our government has the power and ability to end the Korean War instead, they choose greed and power. 

My family from both paternal and maternal is from North Korea. My grandmother fled alone, by herself leaving her entire family behind. She never spoke about her life or family. Today, I walked for my ancestors, for myself and my children. When we marched, shouted, screamed, and chanted, I felt my throat swell up with tear filled eyes. 

Connecting and meeting with so many has filled my heart with joy. The energy and passion of our elders, our friends, and the community have completely changed me forever. 

As we marched from the White House to the Lincoln memorial, clouds rolled in and rained, giving relief with the hot weather. Then, as we progressed with rally, the clouds cleared, and the sky was glorious. A sign that our spirits and ancestors walking among and fighting with us 🙏🔥

#koreandiaspora #koreanamerican #endthekoreanwar #koreanwar #onekorea #womencrossdmz #koreapeacenow #koreapeaceaction #washingtondc #queersforonekorea #ancestors

posts.caption:
Homemade 막걸리, my mom grew up making makgeolli Korean rice wine. My maternal family was rice merchants and farmers, making their own rice wine for casual drinks and celebrations. 

It's so much stronger and a bit vinegar-like. Have you tried homemade version? 
We take the leftover grains from the makgeolli, cook it on stove top with a little water and sugar to make a porridge 술찌꺼기 or 술찌게미 . My mom said on cold winter mornings, the boozy grain porridge would be eaten as breakfast.After 3 spoonfuls, I was ready to lay down for a nap. 

Mom shared that working in the fields under hot sun, folks would gather for communal lunch and to drink makgeolli. Some would dance, sing, and party, while others would be laid out across the rice fields, too drunk to work. 🤣

Have you tried homemade makgeolli? 
It's super strong. 

We use makgeolli rice wine to make offerings to the spirits and guardians of the land. The rice wine is made with rice harvested from the fields and used as offerings to the village guardians, various land spirits, and house spirits. 

Pic 1: homemade rice wine makgeolli in a cup
Pic 2: rice and grains used to make makgeolli rice wine, being cooked on stovetop to make porridge.

posts.caption:
Saying good morning to all the plants and medicine I grow.  I learned from my grandparents how to work and cultivate with the earth. 

In Korea, a special type of soil known as loess or hwangto - used for beauty products, house building and shamanic ceremonies. 

We use earth, soil and dirt in rituals and ceremonies to create boundaries and pathways depending on the purpose.  Used throughout history in rituals for prosperity, fertility, protection, and blessings. 

This Wednesday 6/21 Summer Solstice equivalent to the lunar celebration of Dano, or Surnitnal "day of the gods". The 5th day of the 5th lunar month, with celebration ceremonies lasting all week long. I wrote more about Dano and some of the ritual practices in my email newsletters sent out last night and in my free e-magazine Musok Life (link in bio to sign up). 

Picking any plant for medicine or spiritual workings on Dano is said to be potent with energy. Mugwort is picked and strung into bundles that are hung above in doorways (threshold), or worn as a tiger amulet for spiritual protection. 

The yang energy of Dano is the perfect time to work on intentional practices, ritual workings, and any projects or goals. 

Happy Dano, Summer Solstice ☀️ 

Pictured: borage flowers, chamomile, elderberry, chives, sugar snap peas, blueberries, lemon, tomatoes, roses and raspberry.

posts.caption:
Happy Mothers day - to moms, caretakers, parents, community mothers, and spiritual mothers. 

Mother's Day is weird for me, complicated and numb. 
I didn't grow up with my mom, making cards and gifts at school when mom wasnt there. The last thing I saw was her back as she walked out the door. I didn't know at that time that it would be the last time I saw her. We reunited later in life but I had many caretakers throughout my life - random family members of aunts and cousins. 

I met my spirit mother (elder) when I was still healing from my maternal wounds. She was understanding and listened to my life stories, I felt seen and heard. 

Looking back, I may have grown up without my mom - but I gained love from my community mothers. Being a mom, a parent is tough - it's forced me to look at my struggles and pushed me to rise above. 

Sending power and warmth to all the parents, caretakers, moms, matriarch, community, and spiritual mothers. 

Pic 1 - pregnant me with my first son 2013
Pic 2 - one of the few pics of mom and me 
Pic 3 - my spirit mom and elder

#mothersday

posts.caption:
The last few weeks and months have been illuminating. It's been a rollercoaster of many emotions and discovery. 

I have a hard time trusting people, but when I let do, I openly share. There's been a relationship I've been struggling with, and my senses told me to protect myself. I thought our biggest issues were boundaries, but little did I really know. 

All the jokes and little comments about my appearance, gender expression, gender identity, and whatever you else you felt entitled to say was never coming from "a good place", or as a friend. 

Then it hit me, the realization - the spiral, knowing the truth. This has been going for months, and possibly longer. I mourned. Not for you but for myself. I denied my knowing and denied the prickly feelings that I had.

I have been processing through art and creative expression. What was meant to derail and distract me, I'm using to fuel to go into my work deeper. The things I was too scared and shy about, I'm exploring and sharing. Collaborating with others, saying yes to opportunities, and really working in community and shared spaces. Shit happens and I'm grateful for these teaching moments and lessons - to listen to my inner voices and feelings. 

#growth #friendship #shithappens #mudangjenn

posts.caption:
I said no, no, no. 

A university in France reached out. They wanted me to speak and teach their Korean studies class about shamanism. Until they wanted my labor for free. They said they didn't have funding in their budget for my time and labor. I declined. 

 I was supposed to teach a winter course on Korean art, literature and culture studies sharing our shamanism. Until it was time to review the budget, they didn't want to compensate for my time/labor. Apparently, being a Christian school, viewed this overseas course as a missionary trip. That's a big no.

I said no to everything. 
I always wanted to teach, thought about going back to school to teach. 

A blessing in disguise. 
Truthfully, I felt conflicted. 
I wanted to teach Korean diaspora, not white Christian students. 

This experience helped me realign my goals and thoughts. I don't need to teach at academic institutions to be valid. After working with a few professors and researchers, these academic spaces are not open to learning, but their interest is in reinforcing their narratives. 

When the researcher submitted their work on my story as a Korean American mudang, it was edited because my story and experience was too fringe. My story was a bit wild to be accepted, and edited to fit the conservative narrative. 

This year I've been saying no. 
No - to things that's doesn't align with me. 
No - to people that doesn't value me
No - to friends who weren't

I say no so I can make room for FUCK YES! 
Saying no, made space for so much more. 

#koreanshaman #mudangjenn #koreanstudies #academic #koreanspirituality #asianamerican #boundaries #growth 
#koreandiaspora #gods #goddess #ancestors #deities #musok #mugyo #shamanism #애동제자 #신수보살 #무당젠 #뉴욕무속 #뉴욕무당

posts.caption:
Despite the popularity of shamanism and our practices. It's still technically illegal in Korea, I learned. 
Yes, even though laws says freedom of religion but they make the practices of shamanism difficult for legal recognition. 

For tax purposes shamanism isn't acceptable, its often why shamans use Buddhism as a front, or blend into their practice to be more legitimate. The laws is more acceptable with Buddhist practices than shaman practices. 

I initiated during a time of conflict, when shamanism was being dragged down because of the scandal with President Park 2016. When we traveled around we kept our heads low, made sure we didn't look like mudangs or share anything about ourselves. Keep it low and quiet. 

Korea was protesting. 
Being tucked away in the rural mountains,  I wasn't aware of the chaos that was happening in Seoul. 

And it made me afraid. 
My family fought with me to dissuade me from this path, and now Korea. I felt I had bad luck, I was initiating during a time when there was so much dislike for shamans enough to protest. 
Later, mudangs held their own protest. ✊️

Looking back now. 
It was the perfect damn time to initiate. 
✊️✊️✊️

1: altar with offerings to Dragon King Yongwang shrine in Taebaek mountain. 
2: Dragon King ritual at underwater tomb of Munmu Daewang 
3: Altar preparations at the rental ceremony space on Gyerongsan Phoenix Dragon mountain.

posts.caption:
I use to date a boy who would always make jabs at my family origin. He would joke and say, North Korea is the best Korea - whenever my Korean heritage was brought up. 

I've had many similar experiences with other folks and groups when they mention North Koreans as using derogatory words to minimize their existence. 
I am the eldest daughter, and granddaughter - descendant of North Korean refugees from both my maternal and paternal line. My family settled in Paju (right by the DMZ) in hopes of reuniting with others who might of crossed over. 

Recently I collaborated with a Korean artist in the NYC Wind Folk performance of Seung Taek Lee (이승택). It was an absolute honor to participate in this performance, the artist himself being a North Korean refugee. 
I was a bit disheartened to hear that this performance was commented as commie art by some. When the actual meanings of this performance is to explore the elements of wind and fire - exploration of energy or spirits. 

I'm grateful for the privilege of being the first few Korean Americans to initiate as a mudang shaman.  It has brought me on a journey to explore my ancestral roots and stories, a weaver of the heavenly and earthly. 

A shameless brag but I'm proud of this work because through our NY house and lineage bringing access of ceremonies, rituals and other future baby mudangs into our diaspora communities. 

As Bob always said to me (Jicarilla Apache elder and medicine man) he told me to grow some balls and lead our communities, he reminded me over and over that this was my path and duty. He's crossed over now within the ancestral realm, but he always makes his presence outside my window, visiting as a hawk to remind me to keep going. 🙏😭 
Fly High Bob 🪶

Pic 1: finger pointing towards North Korea mountains at the DMZ
Pic 2: Pic of North Korea landscape from the DMZ
These pictures were taken in Korea 2017

posts.caption:
Spent hours last night in prayers, then pushed out a load of bujeok talisman for my spirit sister. Dropped off both of my boys to school this morning and now, sitting here at a cafe for breakfast, alone - in quietness. 

I enjoy my alone time. I can sit by myself for hours and days in my thoughts, my dream world. While in my thoughts waiting for my order, my day dream was abruptly interrupted when the cashier told me it was $28 for a small espresso and chicken sandwich. Panic and tingles rushed through my body - like holy shit, it's so expensive. 

Born and raised in NYC concrete jungle, I moved into the suburbs just 2-3 years ago. Slowly, our suburban area is being flooded with heavy traffic and insane development. 

Feel the calling of a slower life - a more thoughtful existence. Somehow, I just can't make the decision to uproot the lives of my kids, they are thriving and happy. 

But one day, maybe when my kids are grown and older I will one day go back to the land, the earth. 
Until then, I'm here at this cafe questioning my life's decision on a 28 dollar order of espresso and a chicken sandwich 🐔🥪

Pic 2: Handrawn amulet talisman on top of altar

NYC Lincoln Center
David Rubinstein Atrium
Thursday, March 9th, 7:30PM
Friday, March 10th, 7:30PM

[moim] is the Korean word for gathering! Presented in collaboration with members of KQTx (the first national network for Queer and Transgender folx of Korean descent), you are invited to a two-day symposium of healing, celebration, and affirmation. Join us on March 9 for a panel discussion and Q&A with fabulous community leaders, healers, and organizers. On March 10, we’ll enjoy beautiful performances of personal narrative and queer liberation, culminating in a dance party!

*Masks are required for these events. Though free of cost and open to all, moim is an intentional space that prioritizes Queer and Trans Korean folx. If joining as an ally please be mindful of capacity. moim prioritizes a culture of respect, barring racist, transphobic, anti-Black, xenophobic, classist, ageist, ableist, anti-sex work, or non-consensual behavior.

Reposted: @canalprojectsny 

💥💥 On Saturday, Feb 25 at 3pm we are excited to present a reenactment of Seung-taek Lee’s 1971 performance “Wind-Folk Amusement” in partnership with Hudson River Park. First enacted on Nanji Island on the Han River in Seoul, this NYC iteration will be led by the collaborative duo, Korean-American artists: A young Yu and Nicholas Oh. The performance will take place at Hudson River Park’s Pier 45, at Christopher St. 💥💥

Titled Wind – Folk Amusement, this performance is one of many large-scale outdoor works through which Seung-taek Lee gave form to the transient elements of nature. The intention of the performance is to present a new mode of artistic existence by giving discernable form to invisible air. Through the wavering of long strands of red fabric, Yu, Oh and additional collaborators including Mudang Jenn, will orchestrate a choreography that reveals natural and spiritual phenomena. 🌬🌎

Nervous and Stomach in knots, this is so exciting.

posts.caption:
Let me make this very clear. 

I should of paid more attention - it was in the morning when it was chaos with the kids. Something this important that quotes my work, I realized there was a huge mistake. 

Shamanism is fluid and changed along with the people and society. It's always been meant to use as tools for the people and community within our roots and ancestry. 

Although our practices is open to all. 
The intiatory closed practices of the mudang (shaman) is open to those with roots and ancestry. 

Also in the article stated that I am close contact with a foreigner mudang (whom I won't name) but that is also not true as I am not in any relationships (friendship or working) with any foreigner mudangs. 

I realized it may be too late to revise the publication of the article and need to clarify.

Taking some time to build and create. This week, we experienced a loss in our family, losing an important pillar, the matriarch. My partners grandmother. 

His grandmother was an incredible woman. She's a well known poet and organizer of an underground newspaper during Japanese colonization in China. She was always on the run, targeted by Japanese soliders but she remained viligant and fought using words and power of press. She was a fighter, and her life's work is now turning into a museum. 

I think alot about the oppression and traumas of women and in our communities. Our ceremonial spaces and practice of shamanism and folk magic has been a safe space for women and others marginalized by society. 

This year I'm exploring art and expressive body movements - reclaiming our power and roots. While building all the projects to share with you in our journey to connect and become powered by our spirits and ancestors.

posts.caption:
Important lessons I learned in 2022
- learning to regulate my nervous system
- opening myself to work and collaborate with others (trust issues much? 😅)
- getting over myself

I know I been saying forever. I'm ready to share and teach our spiritual practices. And yet I didnt. 😪

I admit it, my head has been stuck up my ass that alot of times - my thoughts dominate the way I show up. Had the realization that I need to get over myself and the obstacles my thoughts/mind set up. 
Began to process and unpack what my work really is - which is to share with you the powers of our spiritual and ancestral practices. 

Samje 삼재 is an astrological cycle that comes into everyone's saju (Korean astrology chart) I guess it's kinda like a Saturn return in western astrology. I'm currently in my samje - although challenging, it's been really powerful! Helping me by showing where I need growth. 

Learning to come back into our bodies is important. Our spiritual practices has been teaching us to be present in our bodies. 

This year for 2023 - it's not about me, while being about me (and thats ok). I was so worried about taking up space, being too much, being wrong, saying the right words and blah blah blah. Mental noise. So over that. 

My energy has shifted, and my focus has realigned with sharing with the community. Thanks for your patience while I got my shit together. 
Now let's get to work.⚡️

Subscribe to my email and sign up on my website.
I will be asking the community questions and sharing news and projects. 🙂

I appreciate you, grateful to everyone.

posts.caption:
Folk story/mythology of red beans on Winter Solstice. 

Traditions of red bean porridge can be traced back to 1046 BC to the Zhou Dynasty. The story goes the young son of Gong Gong hated red beans and died on Winter Solstice. His son turned into a plague spirit. To ward off the disease spreading spirit, people began to put out and scatter red bean around their homes. 

There are 3 different types of Dongji depending on the it's date: Aedongji, Jungdongji and Nodongji. 
Korea used to celebrate Winter Solstice as their new year until 1309 when Goryeo switched to the Shoushi Calendar during Yuan Dynasty. During Winter Solstice it was believed that Koreans turned a year older on Dongji after eating a bowl of patjuk.

Calendars and quilted socks were given as gifts to promote good luck.

posts.caption:
Arkward face. 
I just finished doing a podcast the other day with the talented @ymmayer and the @hairybuttholepodcast. Where I talked about some of my childhood trauma and my lived experience growing up in an abusive and authoritarian household. 

Grateful to speak about my experiences and how that influenced me. 
After recording, I went into a spiral and began to worry about the things I said/shared. Which is normal because it's just my reaction to being vulnerable. Being vulnerable can feel really icky, but it's a reminder that I'm human. Being vulnerable is powerful and sacred. 

I struggled alot with taking space in any capacity. I would hide and even afraid of my own shadow at times. But my grandmother spirit told me that I'm not helping or contributing by staying hidden in darkness. And slowly, she gave me the courage to step out - doing so has been incredibly transformative and healing for me. 

Thank you so much again to @ymmayer and @hairybuttholepodcast @joysauceofficial
Podcast episode coming out this Friday 12/24 New moon.

Photographic Justice: Tribute to Corky Lee led by curator Chee Wang Ng 12/15 at the US District Court for the Eastern District of NY - Brooklyn NY. 

Corky Lee was a huge community activist and photographer for Chinatown and Asian community. "Lee inspired a generation of Asian American photographers and community activists to document the life and struggles of everyday Asain American and fight against injustice, inequality,  stereotyping and discrimination..." 

I had the honor meeting Corky through my partner - a personal friend and photographer mentor. 

Thank you @jaimesunwoo for the invitation. This event is organized through the AAAYA (Assoc of Asian American Yale Alumni) this is open to anyone interested.

posts.caption:
Traditional shamanism involves worship of heaven (king of heaven) a 'masculine' form of Korean shamanism.  Whereas the 'feminine' form believe in working with the earth spirits (nature) and ancestors. 

It's often looked down upon and viewed as a derogatory form of shamanism because 'worshipping the heavens' is considered to be a higher hierarchy. 

I will be discussing more about these narratives and the  origin myths of a mudang (Korean shaman). It's important to understand our ancestral stories while being critical about it.

After a Friday night out, the next day we had kut 굿 ceremony. For many years -  like a shadow, I followed my spirt mother everywhere. Spent all my days and time with her. 

Maintaining a schedule has been the greatest challenge.  We can be called into ritual/ceremony without much notice. Then I'm scrambling to adjust my schedule accordingly. 
Just want to say thank you to everyone for their patience when I need to reschedule.

I just need to sit down and focus.

posts.caption:
Currently in Jeonju, and visited Jeonbuk National University with my researcher friend. It was amazing to tour different shrines and cultural places here. 

I had the upmost privilege of meeting with National Cultural Heritage mudangs here. I was embraced with kind warmness as we discussed our traditions, ceremonies and the role of mudangs. They shared so much wisdom 🙏🏽❤️ with me. 
They opened their doors to me and offered their space whenever I visit Korea. I feel my prayers been answered, my spirits have always made things happen. 

We also got word today that the research paper that's written about New York Mudangs (whoo-hoo represent!!) was just accepted by the International Conference of Anthropology, and will be presented in Taiwan! So grateful, incredibly blessed. 😭🙏🏽

posts.caption:
The core of our shamanic practices and folk magic is family. 

It's because of my young ones, my family that I walk this path either as a shaman or as folk magic worker. It's always been the songs of matriarch hearts that's echoed in us, our beings. 
You don't need to have a special intiation, or magical abilities to have impact as a future ancestors. You are the spirit pillar. 

I been exploring folk magic because I believe in the power of our matriarchs. I've thought that being initiation as a shaman meant that we were super special - but we are not. It's our position as matriarchs within our families that is so special and powerful.

I've been told by so many people like scholars, shamans and men that our folk magic isnt powerful. That it's all just superstitions, and only us shamans have power. 
That is not fucking true. That's rooted in patriarchy, misogyny, elitism and so many other isms. 
I believe in the magic of our matriarchs, the traditions of our folk magic that our shaman practices were birthed from. I believe that we all have access to spirits and each of us will express it in different ways. 

The way to release han, and the different layers of han is through your storytelling - and no one gets to tell the stories of you, your family and ancestors better than you.

posts.caption:
When Confucian patriarchal scholars try to dictate what is wrong or right - "that's the language of oppressors. " (Credit to my friend Victoria.therese)

When navigating theses academic spaces it's heavily  patriarchal, and it's been been 🤯😵‍💫. One particular scholar asserts himself as the knowledge holder of all things Korean Shamanism and it's questionable (my personal opinion). 

Its problematic when this scholar wields control and misguided authority - and shamans and diaspora's flock to him for connection and access. He proudly stated that he does not give permission for mudangs to enter to do ceremonies or prayers while looking down on diaspora's. 

For the sake of research, I held an open mind, but it's has been causing troubling ruckus within me. What is the point of academic research within our spiritual traditions? Is it to control and dictate while promoting nationalism or is it purely just research to record the stories of tradition?

posts.caption:
My parents home garden is stunning. 
Walking through fields and gardens is a childhood memory of mine spending time with my grandmother. 

I spent my childhood in a community garden. Asian elderlies took a city dump and transformed it into a garden. They would use whatever materials in the dump to repurpose into borders, trellises, and whatever else. Each person had their area, and each grew their own crops and vegetables to either sell on street or for their own family.

posts.caption:
BIPOC Offering ONLY !! 

A huge thank you to @hags_1111 Hannah Kim for this workshop and offering. I'm excited!!!!! If you wish to take this course please message for scholarships if experiencing any hardships. 

Class Description: "Celebrating the 40th anniversary of this seminal publication, we will study Theresa Hak Kyung Cha’s Dictee along with some of its academic critique. This work in many ways defies categorization–with its mixture of French and English, text and images, and the poetic and political. Though it has been described variously as an autobiography, a postcolonial text and an avant-garde, experimental work, it still remains largely inscrutable. Through academic critique and discussion, we will seek to unearth some of its many layers and better understand its contribution to the Asian American literary canon."

I just recently bought this book have already felt the words and poetry flow into my body and mind. I been thinking of Theresa work daily. 
I will be taking up the offering, I hope to see you there too.

COVID is rampant here. 
It's been blazing through my son's classroom. 
More of his classmates, friends and teachers are getting sick. The other day at dismissal they were handing us Covid test - only to my son's class. 
Today the school called us, his classes are cancelled and urged us to get tested. 

What are we doing? 
We just had a shooting here where people were killed at the supermarket. And now children (same age as my Mason) gunned down. 

What the hell are we doing. 
How can any question, fight or even argue against protecting our children. 

Alot of parents messaged me asking me for bulletproof bookbags. I found out the Level IIIA bookbag armor plates are only meant for handguns and useless against assault rifles and automatics which are used for these shootings.

In partnership with Jennifer Kwon Dobbs, author and Professor of English affiliated with Race and Ethnic Studies, Gender and Sexuality Studies, and Family Studies. Her teaching interests include poetry, poetics, creative nonfiction, Asian American literature, and critical ethnic studies. 

We are creating an off-campus study course for St. Olaf College focused on Muism (Korean Shamanism) in art, literature, and culture! This summer, we will head to Seoul to develop infrastructure and conduct research with January 2024 in mind for the course's launch.
We will be leaving July and return August from our research and site locations.

A step closer bringing access and teachings of Korean shamanism and it's folk magic practices. 
Represent!!! 

Deep gratitude to Jennifer for setting this up and giving the opportunity to create a course to explore Musim - Korean Shamanism. Forever grateful. 🙏🏽🙂
To St. Olaf College for their support and funding for this research and course creation. 

Minnesota, I will see you soon

posts.caption:
I'm going to Korea!!! 🇰🇷 만세!!! 
Ahhhhhh. 

I planned on traveling to Korea this year but I had difficulties with aligning my schedule and finances. Airfare tickets were almost $2500 😨. I wasn't able to travel with my spirit family for prayers, pilgrimage and ceremony. I was pretty bummed and really wanted to go. 

Then somehow, someway the spirits and ancestors made it possible. A miracle happened. 
Praise the ancestors and spirits!!! 
I been given an opportunity to teach, with all expenses paid and funded to Korea for research!!! 
(Can I now call myself a researcher?) Hahah. 

I've struggled alot with being open to receiving. 
Whether it's praise, love, money, help or whatever form - Ive been resistant to opening myself. Slowly bit by bit I am learning to be more open, to receiving and to just flow. 
It's a struggle that many of us experience. 
I do too. 

My grandmother taught me not to spend my time growing weeds in a garden but to be intentional and plant the seeds of growth. 

Shit. 
I'm going to Korea. 🇰🇷
To my ancestors Halmoni, Haraboji - I'm coming. 😭

posts.caption:
Happy Mother's Day. 

My two boys has been screaming "Happy Mother's Day" all morning. Mother's Day has always been weird for me, when everyone in elementary class making cards for their mom. I just drew and scribbled because I didn't have my mom. 

My parents were divorced at 9. The moment my mom walked out - l became mom to my siblings. Years later, I reunited with mom and our relationship has been hard and rough. Becoming a mother myself, I began to understand mom more and that helped me on my healing journey.

Im grateful for my mom, and even more because of the love and care she gives my boys. 

And then to my godmother/spirit mother, my other mother. I been so blessed to have her in my life, who opened her arms and brought me in with the family. She helped me become the person I am today, the mudang that I am. Forever grateful. 

the journey of motherhood is hard but also fills you.

posts.caption:
Posted @withregram • @davidjshi311 I just received this book “Spell Bound” from my friend @chaweonkoo.  To say I’m blown away is an understatement.  This book navigates witchcraft/spirituality and Asian-American identity in the modern world.

As @shaman.mudang has said in her post, occult, spirituality, and witchcraft spaces have been overwhelmingly white.  This book is significant not only for representation, but also answers a deep identity trauma that haunts all Asian-Americans.  To many Americans, we are not American.  To many Asians in Asia, we are not Asian enough.  For those of us who hunger for spiritual practice, most spiritual spaces in the U.S. either don’t acknowledge our spiritual heritage, grossly simplify to Hollywood Buddhism & Taoism, or even worse just don’t welcome us.  Several months ago, someone in a Facebook witchcraft group declared that the Asian 5-element system “made absolutely no sense”. Sure, several of us have dived deep into our ancestral practices, but we as the diaspora are not in Asia, we are in the U.S. land and must contend with the spirits/energies here as well as from Asia.  There is extremely little that addresses Asian-American spiritual identity.

And yet, this is exactly what Chaweon has done.  This work is technically a book, but is so much more.  It is a ritual in the form of a book, with an opening rite, an exploration into the Asian five elements, and a closing rite.  Seeing that alone, the acknowledgement and lessons of the five elements in witchcraft, is powerful.  Each section intertwines her own personal experiences, traditional Korean spirituality & shamanism, other traditional Asian practices, Asian-American identity, western witchcraft, and the modern technology landscape together.  While this book contains much traditional knowledge, that’s not its primary purpose.. those are contexts that plunge into the depths of Asian-American spirituality.  Spell Bound is a cathartic experience.

I was pleasantly surprised to see myself quoted… and Mudang Jenn, I see you within the pages as well!

#witchcraft #witch #spellbound #asianamerican #spirituality #mudang #shamanism #korean #koreanwitch #무당 #마녀 #aapi

posts.caption:
Seollal (설날) is the celebration of yang energy. The welcoming of the Lunar New Year. 

DaeBoreum (대보름) is the celebration and welcoming of the yin energy. We greet the moon goddess. 

On the eve of the full moon, hide your shoes. Its said the spirits will roam trying to take away your bok 복 (luck, blessings and fortune) by stealing your shoes. 

You can hang baskets and sieves as spirit traps by your entrances and doorways. Ghosts will be enamored by the holes and will be stuck there counting (spirit trap) till sun rise. 

Burning old hair or red chili pepper is a deterrent for spirits and their pollution. You can spread the ashes outside around your home. 

Making a bonfire or lighting a small candle with a wooden wick is an alternative to the big fire celebrations. The crackling of the wood is exorcistic. Remember to write wishes or prayers and to burn in the fire so that ashes are carried to the heavens and the celestial deities.

Moon divination by interpreting the way the moon rises, its color and other elements like clouds and the sky. Playing with fire embers in tin cans, selling your body heat. These are all practices of our magic magic and traditions. 

In Korean saju astrology, I am yang earth mountain. Seen as mother earth, protector and holder of all elements. Mountains are known for their wisdom, energy and stability. This year with the yang water tiger - it causes the mountain to move. Aligned with the energies of this year and what my spirits and deities have been pushing me to do - its gonna be a busy year.

Daeboreum 대보름 is a huge celebration of the first full moon of the New Lunar year. 
Food is one of the ways to take part in the folk magic practices and rituals. Through food we are able to connect to families, friends, neighbors and most importantly ancestors. 

We eat special dishes of dried vegetables and prepare rice with grains and beans. We crack nuts and drink liquor on this day to celebrate. The dried nuts and vegetables symbolize the abundance of harvest. 

Many have asked about special rituals and ceremonies you can do in your personal practice. Food can be the vehicle to help explore our history, stories and spiritual practices.

posts.caption:
The first Korean calendar after liberation from the Japanese occupation, power and control. Circa 1946. 

It was during the Japanese occupation that the celebration of 설날 Seollal (Lunar New Year) was banned. Instead the Japanese changed lunar New year to the gregorian 1/1 at attempts to disconnect our roots and culture. 

Wearing traditional colors like red, white and saekdong (5 colors) celebrate the New Year. 
•Red to greet the yang energies of the sun, warding off evil. 
•Saekdong (5 colors) was used in alot of children's hanboks as a form of protection. 
•White to represent the Sun and the heavens. Korean was always known as the people who wore white - this custom dated back to ancient times up until recent modernity (80's or 90's). 

☆Learn more about 설날 Seolall in my upcoming workshop discussing the folk magic, traditions and history.

posts.caption:
Thank you so much for asking about this @sadqueerme . 

When I talk about mudangs, I mean specifically charismatic kangsingmu mudangs. This specific type requires 내림 (naerim) or 신굿 (spirit ceremony). 

Not all mudangs, shamans or spiritual workers are the same, each have their owns skills, specialty and ability. It can becomes dangerous when the mudang isn't aware. 

You will need to have a consultation with a experienced mudang to determine that. Its important your ancestors are channeled correctly because they will show up in the reading. 

Some people are called to ancestors, and work with them. Other may be called  and become a mudang (initiated) but does no shaman work. Or others get initiated and walk this path fully like myself because we aren't allowed to do anything else. When we get initiated we say 신의 매달려. Means to hang on and believe in spirit. Its been rough but its made me into the person I am. 

If you do decide to do rituals make sure that person is trained. Ceremony always involves others with an elder. 

I hope helps a bit. And will speak more about this in detail.
