I have a VERY huge problem with Korean 무당 Shamans initiating white academic scholars. I came across something incredibly disturbing. I'm shocked and appalled for many numerous reasons. I've sat on it, contemplated it, thought alot about it and I simply cannot condone it. ⁣
Based on posts and pictures of the 내림굿 naerim kut ceremony, I see so many things that raises red flags.  Even question the legitimacy of all this.⁣
⁣ • The so-called initiation ceremony had the initiate sitting in a chair, wearing a normal tunic and pants. ✋ Stop, what?  A shaman initiation ceremony with NO shaman regalia or robes - none? Plus shes not even wearing hanbok 한복 for her initiation. The basics of what is needed in an initiation ceremony is - omitted.⁣
⁣ • The OFFERINGS! Oh my dear. How is that an offering table for the gods? Of an initiation?? The damn PIG is missing! 😱 Where is 대감 in this initiation 내림굿? There is absolutely  no good excuse for the poor offerings. Only fruit was present. Couldnt find any rice, vegetables, meat or tofu? I mean, was the supermarket closed? - or just plain no accountability? ⁣
⁣
• Where is the ANCESTORS? Did you guys forget to send the invites to the ancestors? Where is their offerings, their hanbok clothes? How can there be an initiation 내림굿 without the ancestors? Umm. Trying to wrap my head around it. ⁣
You do know, a proper initiation ceremony to happen, ancestors must come and release their han. Regardless of lineage, or kut styles,  the ancestors must be there. ⁣
This bastardization of a 내림굿 is simply just embarrassing. ⁣
⁣
Do you want to know what's truly sad? -that the true teachers and elders are always in the shadows, unknown to the world. Hard to find, like a needle in haystack.  It's always the ones who have nothing better else to do, that goes prancing around-showing off their simple parlor tricks. ⁣
⁣
Clearly this "initiation ceremony " was certainly NOT about preserving the sacred traditions. Because all those offerings, ritual clothes, and an ancestors are symbolic and KEY necessary ingredients for a proper 굿 ceremony, let alone a damn  initiation.  I wonder with what intentions did the "initiate", a white woman in her 60's have.

posts.caption:
Today is the official day for Chilseong worship rite and ritual. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Chilseong [칠성], the "Seven Star" shamanic deity of the Big Dipper constellation, is depicted with 7 male figures but treated as one god and deity. [Chilseong] is thought to be the protector of the Korean people.  Governing the lifeline longevity of the people, health, peace and most importantly, the health and life span of children and adults. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣ Until a child is 7 years old, their health and life line is under the care of Samsin (Goddess Grandmother of childbirth, and protector of infants) After 7 years, it is looked after by Chilseong under their care.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Each person has a white long cloth symbolizing their life line that is dedicated to him/her/they. We pray to the gods asking Chilseong to take these lifelines and care for them. Like gardeners tending to a garden, working with each life life making sure each is maintained, watered and growing with strength.  We ask Chilseong to breathe in new life and vitality to each of the life lines. ⁣
⁣⁣
⁣⁣

posts.caption:
Tomorrow we have a privately sponsored 칠성제 (Chilseong -je) ritual rites. ⁣
⁣
칠정 (Chilseong) is the God(s) of longevity, especially longevity of children. Known as the 7 stars, and their worships one of the oldest rituals. Comes from the Ursa Major constellation [Big Dipper]. Their 'holiday ' is celebrated on the 7th day of the 7th lunar month. ⁣
⁣
The client, an elderly grandmother wanted a private 칠성 ritual rites for the grandchildren in the family. She wanted to make sure the gods, took extra care of her grandchildren. We prepare long white fabrics with each child information signifying their 'life line'. ⁣Asking the gods like a gardener to care and protect their longevity.
⁣
Year after year, we have multiple 굿 (kut) ceremonies for her family throughout. Despite her frail body, to witness her dedication to the spirits and gods through prayers & bows was truly touching.⁣
⁣
🙏🙇‍♀️⁣
[Picture of a 칠성당 Chilseong shrine on 태백산 Mount Taebak, Korea.] ⁣
See the white cloth of 'life lines' the gods are protecting. ⁣
⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
The Sanshin shrine in the Korean Buddhist temple of Jeondeungsa. ⁣
⁣
Koreas mountain worship is found throughout the peninsula. Our shamanic god of the mountain, Sanshin 산신, the mountains is symbolic for the axis of the world. ⁣
Sanshin god of mountain is always depicted with a tiger, and some rarer paintings it would depict 3 tigers. The oldest Sanshin painting is housed in Mount Inwang and roughly dated back to the 1700s. ⁣
산신 are traditionally drawn in a seated position, with a white fan made from the feathers of a white crane. White crane in korean culture is symbolic for high status, longevity, wisdom, etc. Sanshin is always dressed in color red, although some modern paintings have 산신 in other forms and colors. Along with the tiger, 산신 also have children attendees Dong-ja & Dong-yeo. ⁣
⁣
While most mountains and Sanshin are depicted as an elderly man, some mountains in Korea are said to be inhabited by a female Sanshin, a Yeo-Sanshin. The most famous 여산신 (yeo-sanshin) of Korea is 지리산 (Mt. Jiri) and 계룡산 (Mt. Gyerong). Some temples will have 탱화 taeng-hwa (mural) of both male Sanshin god with the female yeo-sanshin. ⁣
⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
Woke up around 4am.⁣
Its prime time for prayers, its supposedly when spirit connection is at its peak. When we go to Korea for pilgrimage, we also pray in the mountains and at sacred shrines at this time. Whenever I am disturbed by spirits or energy, I stir  around this time. ⁣
⁣
When there is no 굿 kut ritual ceremonies scheduled, and I wake at this time. I take it as a sign, a gentle nudge by my gods to "have a chat"...called into prayers. Before I step into my 신당 (shindang; shrine of gods), I must be clean so I hop in for a early morning bath. ⁣
When I enter my 신당, I give my morning greetings. Fresh water offerings are poured, candles are lighted and incense sticks are lit by the candleflames. The flame that lights the incense must never be blown out with our mouth, instead it's much more proper to 'shake' out the flame. It's a mindful and respectful gesture, just like vacuums cleaners are avoided in a temple, instead I use dry swiffer cloths to clean. Every act and behavior within the temple should be very mindful and intentional, it's an act of respect while in the presence of the gods. ⁣
⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
Exorcism. ⁣
To cast out negative energy, clearing and cleansing. ⁣
There many ways to perform an exorcism  from sea salt, to burning red pepper flakes, to cooking up - what I call  exorcism stew 찌개. ⁣
⁣
The exorcism ritual was taught directly to me by my elder. The ritual is perform whenever I needed to remove negative energy or casting out any hitchhiking spirit influences.  I usually call upon the gods, goddess and deities to drive out the negative influences. ⁣
⁣
As I was taught, in my chants, one of things we say is "eat and be gone". It refers to any lowly homeless spirits that may be attached. With the exorcism stew, we tell the spirits to eat and leave. When performing this ritual on other people, we take pieces of their hair and other things. We take all this and 'feed' it to the negative forces.⁣
⁣
My 장군칼, spirit tools and weapons of my warlord generals, cuts any attachments and cleans the space. We throw the knives down, and read the way the knives land looking for indicators of a successful exorcism. ⁣ ⁣Picture taken last fall 2018 in Korea at one of the sacred shamanic prayers sites. ⁣

posts.caption:
Part 2/2⁣
⁣
All the various and different paths of the many 무당 (shaman) is like the unique houses or buildings lined up on a city block. Each house is different, having custom styles and designs. No two house is the same, but then strip away the cosmetics and exteriors. ⁣
Look at their bones and structures they are the same. All built with a sturdy foundation, with supporting walls and a protective roof. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣This is how I view the many paths of 무당's today. My advice is do not replace the sacred, instead add-on to it enriching your practice. For the modern 무당, I say learn the way its been practiced, then bring in your modern elements once you understood the valuable teachings of the tradition. ⁣⁣
(Example, learn to perform divination in traditional way as it helps makes you exercise your ability to establish connection with the gods. Learn to understand the language and tone of the spirits through use of traditional tools. Afterwards teach and work with the spirits to learn the language of modern ways and tools) ⁣
⁣.
.
Obviously this isnt a 'one size fits all'... but it can help find your methods. Some times the gods have something else different planned out than what you want. ⁣
I thought I was going to blend traditional Korean shamanism with modern spiritual practices. Truthfully, traditions scared me. I did not want to fully accept the 'daunting' burden', and wanted to bring in modern elements that made it easier to practice, making it more convenient path to accept and walk. ⁣
⁣
⁣Obviously, my gods had a different plan than I did

Part 1/2

A shamanic apprentice in our culture must devote 3 years of their life to the elder, the teacher before any spiritual lessons begins. It's also to test the initiate strength and determination....because this path isn't rainbows and butterflies. ⁣
⁣
Every 무당 path is different, as their ancestors and their gods are all different. But the basics, the foundations, our core ways and teachings matter on our path.  There are steps to learning things, it's a slow process. Ex: a baby 무당 would learn how to perform an exorcism on self first, gaining experience before trying to do one on a person or place. There is no shortcuts. ⁣
⁣

잡귀 or 잡신⁣
⁣
As a shaman, our spirit door is always open. Walking this world with one foot part of the physical and one foot in the spirited world.⁣ ⁣
잡신 (Japshin) refers to the low energy, dark aura spirit beings. 잡귀 (Jap-gwhi) refers to the heavy dark energy. Because we are shamans in constant contact with spirits, we also encounter 잡귀&잡신. It also very possible for a shaman to be swayed and influenced by 잡신, especially if they lack experience and the know-how's. ⁣
Establishing a strong relationship with your gods and spirits helps keep a 무당 balanced and grounded.⁣ ⁣
It's a known within our world, that you can easily be possessed and influenced by 잡신, when performing mountain rites and prayer for the gods and spirits.  Which is why its usually not advised for learning shamans to alone, and always with an elder. ⁣
⁣

Lunar Eclipse. ⁣⠀
In observance of tonight's eclipse,  thought I share a tale. ⁣⠀
⁣⠀
불개 Bulgae (Fire dogs) are legendary beasts of darkness belonging to one of the Kings of Hell. ⁣⠀
In the Kingdom of Gamangnara (Black land), the King was fed up living in darkness.  He desired light within his dark kingdom. ⁣⠀
The Dark King sent his fire dog to capture the sun. The beast chased the sun and bit down on it. It tried to carry the sun it's in mouth, but ended up burning itself.⁣⠀
The dog returned empty handed, and so the King sent 불개 after the moon. The fire dog determined to succeed, chased the moon down with vigor. It chomped and tried to carry the moon, but it was too cold and made his mouth freeze. The  fire dog gave up and returned back to the Dark world. ⁣⠀
The King however did not give up, and still sends the 불개 after the Sun and Moon. ⁣⠀
⁣⠀
It is believed when there is a solar or lunar eclipse, the dark parts are believed to be covered by the mouth of the Bulgae. ⁣⠀

posts.caption:
The 5 colors of Korean shamanism,  similar to Buddhism and Korean lifestyle.The colors have many meanings and symbolism, which I have discussed and spoken about in my past post. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Divination flags 오방기 (Ohbangi) or 길빨 (Ghilpal)  is divination tools used by Daegam 대감 (God of fortune, prosperity and wealth). Flags arent restricted to 대감 only. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Each color also represents a God or Goddess as well. ⁣
°Red represents 산신 (Sanshin)⁣⁣
°Yellow represents 대신 (Daesin)⁣⁣
°White represents 보살 (Bulsa)⁣⁣
°Green represents 동자/동녀 (Donja/Donyeo)⁣⁣
°Blue represents 대감 (Daegam)⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Despite the flags may have their standard meanings like the direction, season and God association. It will still be difficult for laypeople to try and pull flags for guidance and divination on their own. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣

When we offer liquor to our ancestors, each cup must be poured one at a time, since there is a mini-ritual involved. 
We pour one cup, and above the incense smoke we twirl the liquor THREE times clockwise and then THREE times counterclockwise. Then the liquor is placed on the ancestors altar. 
This is done for each of the ancestors liquor cups. For shamanic kut 굿 ceremony, we have 6 liquor offerings for the ancestors. When all offerings are placed on the altar, you must bow 3 times. 
This is done during ancestral rites known as jesa 제사 also in shamanic ceremony/ritual. Whenever liquor is offered to the ancestors, this does not apply for offerings to the gods.

If a 무당 is born from a 양반 (Yangban aristocrats class), most aristocrat families  would rather kill their child than have him/her accept their fate as a 무당. It would be heavily looked down upon, and would be very difficult to accept, since Mudangs belong to the Cheonmin 천민 class of low, vulgar (dirty) commoner. ⁣
⁣
When becoming a 무당, family ties are broken because after the 내림 (Naerimkut initiation), the initiate is reborn. Human relationship and ties are meaningless if accepting the call of the gods and spirits. ⁣무당 would leave their own families to serve their gods. I have read and heard dozen of stories from older 무당's how they would be force to leave their own children and families. ⁣
⁣
I'm lucky, and I acknowledge my privilege. During the peak of my spiritual madness of my shinbyung (Spirit sickness, Divine illness), I felt the mountains were calling⁣ me. Anxiety would build up, and the urge to abandon and leave my family was strong. My partner feared that he would come home to an empty house, he was anxious that I would leave. ⁣
⁣ ⁣

Picture from Google. ⁣
⁣
Sambok refers to the 3 of the hottest days in the 6th &7th lunar month.  Its known as the 3 Dog days, introduced from China during the Qin dynasty. ⁣
Dog days is distinguished by the forecasted negative yin energy and allowing negative spirits to be active. Thus eating red porridge in Dog days helps repel spirits and safeguarding their safety. ⁣
The traditional 3 special dishes served are red bean porridge,  dog meat soup and ginseng chicken soup along with melons. ⁣
Later on, the traditional red bean porridge was replaced by foods that gave nutrition like the ginseng chicken and dog meat soup. Nowadays, dog meat soup is definitely not in favor although still cherished by older generations. ⁣
⁣
⁣
This Saturday is one of the Dog days.  Unfortunately I wont have time to feed my family the traditional dishes of ginseng chicken soup and red bean porridge due to  a 굿 kut shamanic ceremony/ritual that day. ⁣
⁣
Will you celebrate the observance of Dog Day?⁣

posts.caption:
Sometimes I wonder, if I was born in older times would I still be a 무당?⁣
⁣
I acknowledge the privilege I have been given. With modern convenience the 신내림굿's of todays would of been laughed upon by 무당's of the past. My 내림 (Naerim) was a tough a grueling 3 days of exhaustion but I would of not been able to complete such tests without the strength given to me by the gods. Despite that, would I of passed the test of becoming a 무당 in the past? ⁣
⁣
The 내림굿 initiation ceremony would of been much more intense, the shaman-to-be would be put through painstaking tests, that sometimes would claim their lives in the process. The process was intense and hard because it's to test an initiate determination and perseverance, for me it was...ride or die. Silently begging the spirits to heal me, save me from this life, and I was able to transform all my pain, suffering and anguish into tools of compassion, humility and strength.⁣
You can't undo the gods and ancestors,  once you are initiated it is for life. The spirits doesnt care about your family life or your personal life and/or opinions. ⁣
⁣
원신 (Won shin) the Heavenly true gods, the pure gods, they are cold and ruthless. They require, expect and demand full dedication and arent so "understanding" as our ancestors. ⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
There was a branch of korean shamanism that specifically worshipped Dangun as a god only. Gosindo (way of the ancestral God) , was the ancient form of Dangun worship. 
That sect of Korean shamanism was wiped out and died by the 15th century. The legend of Dangun played a vital role during the Mongolian invasion of Korea, where it helped with national unity and mobilization against. 
Due to the resurgence of Korean nationalism from the invasion and occupation of Japan.  Gosindo 고신도 was reborn as Daejongism during the Japanese occupation, and helped the Korean independence movement. Many controversy due the cult-like sects that arose. 
The roots of Dahn Yoga claims that they have the same practices as Dangun did when he first ruled over Korea . 
Picture taken from Google,  a ceremony/ritual for Dangun with his altar of offerings.

posts.caption:
Its proper etiquette and respectful behavior to never show your back to the gods. When sitting down, even if it's to stretch your legs, never point your toes towards the gods. The mural known as 탱화 taenghwa, has the gods facing towards us. 
When we spent 2.5 weeks straight in a 굿 당 we slept, ate, showered and lived in the shrine. During our times spent within the temple/shrine it was difficult to be mindful of such proper behavior and respectful etiquette. 
When we lay the blankets down to sleep, we made sure that everyone was parallel to the painting. Obviously as we toss and turn in our sleep, waking up with our feet pointed towards the gods. Immediately we stand up, and bow our heads and body in a sleepily groggy state to say sorry to the gods. 
Mudang have rigid and strict structures, the daily task of temple/shrine upkeeping. We play a concert maestro, making sure our gods are happy, and synced in harmony. When we work, moving as one fluid spiritual being, a cohesive relationship.

posts.caption:
My elder (spirit mother) shared a story with me, its lasting impression echoing the teachings. ⁣
A mother brought her teenage son (16 yrs) to have his 사주 Saju read, a divination reading. Spirit mom started to unravel the child's chart and she began to explain to the mother. She said the child was intelligently gifted, and if guided and channeled properly, he will grow fortune and money wont be a problem. They discussed many other things including the family business, health, etc. ⁣
⁣
Years later, spirit mom was meeting with clients for divination. A frail looking woman came to have her divination reading. During the reading the woman began to yell at my spirit mother for lying, asking her why her son isnt rich, etc. ⁣
Spirit mom got upset, and soon the the gods yelled at the woman. Do not blame us because your son was lazy, he had the destiny and opportunity to have wealth. Her son was there when my spirit mother spoke of his bright future. The son thought that his future was something set in stone, and opportunities will fall from the heavens along with bags of money. So he sat at home, waiting for things to happen...time would pass, and blessings did not fall from the Heavenly skies. ⁣
I will discuss more specifically about Destiny VS fate in the next coming posts. ⁣
⁣

Picture taken in Korea.
Nov 2018
Pictured here is a shrine dedicated to Sanshin (god of mountain & earth) along with his Tiger and bird spirit poles.

In our traditions,  its is respectful that the elders of the home eat first. As a shaman, as someone who works with the gods and spirits, they eat first. When I go grocery shopping,  my spirits get the first offerings of any fruit, candy, bakery, etc. 
A shaman is an empty shell, a living instrument and vessel for our gods and deities. We live a life of service to the spirits, working in harmony. ⁣
⁣Traditions requires discipline and utmost dedication, with constant teachings of humility. ⁣

So today,  I wanted to give thanks and gratitude to my gods and spirits for "growing me" and guiding me. I had pumpkin jeon (fritters), with korean squash picked from my garden. I set my offering, along with water and liquor as I went into my prayers. I ask for compassion and forgiveness, as I am lacking in many ways. But I give my spirits and gods, thanks and gratitude for providing and protecting for my family and myself. I also put prayers for those whose candles are on my altar, may the gods continue to protect and bless them. 📿🕯 ⁣

Today's altar offering. We have a very special shamanic 굿 kut ceremony. ⁣
⁣
It's called a jinogwhi kut. A special ceremony/ritual to aid the dead into the spirit world. When we set a special table for the recently departed. ⁣
⁣
In the adjacent room, we have additional offering tables set for the guest of the ancestors, and for the ancestors themselves. The offerings for the ancestors is so grand that it takes 2 tables put together. ⁣
⁣
During the kut ritual, we call back the soul/spirit of the recently departed. We allow the spirit to come into our body, as the energy takes over. Then we help usher the 7 parts of the deceased soul into the spirit world. ⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
There are lines even as a mudang 무당, I cant cross. ⁣
⁣
A year or so ago, in a divination....I saw that my stepfather had a dark spot between his chest and stomach. He's  been going to doctors and getting tests done, to find the root cause. ⁣
⁣
Surgery is now schedule in 2 weeks, over half of his stomach needs to be removed. And its quite possibly it has already spread to the liver, but doctors wont say until they open him. They wont confirm what stage he's in, until they open. ⁣
⁣
I knew the winds of samje 잠제 known as the Three Calamities was already starting to shake him. I have experienced and witness how scary 삼재 can be. I tried to convince my mother to have a 병굿 done for him, she declined. ⁣
I spoke to my spirit mother to discuss the possibility of going to perform a Sanshin rite in the mountains. I asked if we set up offerings, drumming and invoking the gods there in the mountains...would it help my step father. I explained my plan was to sit my mother down, discuss and split the cost for this Mountain prayer ritual. ⁣
That's when my spirit mother spoke of my kind heart. She said my kindness could inspire my spirits to help aid. She said all we can do is pray.⁣
I was to told to take a step back, spirit mother said that this is the destiny between them. Whatever it may be. Their choices, their karma, their destiny. ⁣
⁣
⁣
So prayers are up tonight, and every night for him. ⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
When we have a 고사 (gosa) for a place of business, then each entrance/exit will have an offering of red bean rice cake, and a cup of makkoli (rice wine). If there is a kitchen within the business,  another offering is set for the kitchen godess Jowangshin 조왕신. ⁣
⁣
If it's a place with many machinery and power tools, like of a contractor or a warehouse,  we set the offerings of rice cake and makkoli at each location. ⁣
The red bean in our korean shamanic culture are used to perform exorcism, cleansing and chasing of any negative energy and luck. The red bean rice cake serves as a food offering that wards off negativity and lowly bad spirits. ⁣
To bring in luck, prosperity and fruitful blessings a pig offering, is necessary. Depending on the price paid by the client, if the client wanted a super grand gosa, then we would of used a whole pig, or even a whole cow. On top of that meat offerings, we put money dipped in makkoli all over the offerings. ⁣
When leaving money to the mudang, during a gosa. Its proper respect and customary to put an envelope on top of the red bean rice cake (as shown)⁣
⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
I was up by 5:40, and out my door by 6AM.  We packed up the car with all our gears and equipment.⁣
⁣
Today we had a request to perform a 사업고사 in Westchester, NY. The client, Mrs. Yi had a 고사 done 5 years ago performed by my spirit mother, when she was first setting up her shop. ⁣
Every land, place or property has spirits...spirits attached to the land, and along with local gods, deities,  guardian and homeless spirits. ⁣
To make peace, we set up offerings on a temporary altar within the place of business. We drum and chant our mantras, songs and prayers. We tell the local gods, deites and spirits to open the path of blessings and prosperity for this client.⁣
6 months ago, she had another gosa performed with another mudang because it was cheaper. Instead of business flowing and flourishing, she ran into alot of difficulties. Her employees began fighting amongst themselves, customers fighting, having issues with equipment breakdown, legal issues, health issues, etc. She said, she felt as if she was at the beach, getting hit by waves after waves. ⁣
⁣
By the time we packed up and cleaned up, after our gosa ceremony, the door bell rang. A woman appeared and ask if she and 5 others, come in for services. Mrs. Yi was so elated and happy. ⁣
As our car pulled out of the parking. Mrs.Yi began bowing, deep traditional whole body bows at my spirit mother, expressing her deep gratitude. ⁣
I am truly proud of the work we do, and I find it amazing that I am learning directly under a spirit mother, a mentor whom I look up to, and hope to emulate. ⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
Today is World Refugee Day. ⁣⁣
I am a child of immigrants parents, and my parents are children of refugees. When the Korean war erupted, my maternal grandmother left her entire family behind. She embarked on a solo journey on foot climbing over mountains walking towards the South. She never realized that our ancestral land would be divided. She pass away without ever seeing or hearing from her family. ⁣⁣
Stories like my grandmother is common among our grandparents generation. Our parents suffered as post war babies, with little to no food and clothes. ⁣⁣
Today in America, the Trump administration has locked up infants, young children and teens in groups without proper food and water. I read the news today about a young 2 year old toddler, sick with the flu, diaperless and being looked after the older children. ⁣My heart broke for that child and others. ⁣
I remember many times in my life when I wished someone spoke out for me, stood up for me and protected me. It was until I got older that I had to stand up for myself, voicing myself. Now that I am the adult, I hope to be....what I didnt have when I was young. ⁣⁣
⁣In a world, where thousands of families with children are fleeing for their lives, if you can please help donate any funds to help the migrant children. If you cant donate money, find the nearest local refugee resettlement agency and donate goods there. ⁣⁣
⁣
⁣
Picture taken at 강천사, 전라북도⁣
Gangcheonsa,  Jeolla-bukdo⁣
Autumn November 2018⁣

posts.caption:
Born and raised in NYC. ⁣
I never ever like to go into the city, I avoid it like the plague. It's been a few years since I been in the city. ⁣
⁣
My destination today takes me to lower Manhattan by the World Trade Center.⁣
⁣
The WTC stood on top of the graves of 20,000+ slaves. 100's of boxes of artifacts were recovered, and in them what they assume to be Islamic prayer beads. When the land is filled with trauma and chaos, or what we call HAN, the spirits and land are unrested. ⁣
The the tragedy of 9/11 occur spilled more blood and lives lost on this sacred grounds. ⁣
⁣
My trip to Manhattan was not pleasant, turning at the wrong corner, putting in the wrong address on the GPS, getting off the wrong floor of the elevator, etc. Not a good day at all. I was overwhelmed by the heaviness and dizzy spells I was experiencing walking past the WTC. ⁣
⁣
First thing I did when I got home, was an exorcism and house clearing. I can usually tell how bad the buildup of negative energy is.  When I use my 장군칼 (General warlord knives) for exorcism, I get sick all over again as I perform the clearing⁣
⁣
**of course, I take a turn and now standing next to a cemetery. ⁣

Mr & Mrs. Vangsavath are devoted and faithful followers of Buddhism. Despite Laos being an strong animist country, shamans are still something very rare, and hard to find...as I was told. ⁣
The older generations viewed shamans like old superstition, and the client Mr. Vangsavath parents were uneasy about us, mudangs and shamans. Talking of the spirits and ancestors who passed didnt really strike a good chord with the parents, but despite their indifference.....they trusted us, believed in us. ⁣
They knew about the work we had done for Mia's son Skyler.  Mrs.Vangsavath had witness firsthand the changes and transformation that Sklyer went through with his disease/sickness 병굿, putting their faith in us. ⁣
 Even though our divination session was through video, her ancestors were already in my home communicating with me. Especially the grandfather, I stayed up because of him, restless. He told me different things but his focus and attention was on his rice fields. He kept asking me what happened to them, as he went on about stories from the rice paddies. ⁣
I asked the client about the grandfather stories and rice field, she wasnt sure and never heard of such things from the elders. She later confirmed with me, after asking her mother in law. The rice paddies she told me, is still in the family tended by the aunt. This made her mother dislike us even more, since she disapproved of "spirit talk". Despite her disapproval, she still trusted us to work in our ways to bring healing to her family. For that I am eternally grateful to the gods, deites and ancestral spirits that help us create new destinies.

posts.caption:
The sounds of 굿 [KUT or GUT]⁣
Kut or Gut, our shamanic ritual ceremony,  where the mudang serves as a vessel to embody the gods. As the music is played, the gods are called and invoked. ⁣
The gods are invited and called down by the mudang during the 굿. We communicate and express the gods through songs and dance.⁣
⁣
⁣
These are my spirit grandparents of our lineage, the elders. ⁣
Spirit grandma comes from a long line of mudang shamans. Most of her family, her siblings, and extended family are mudangs and baksu (Male shaman). ⁣
Spirit grandpa was a established Buddhist monk, working with the musical instruments. ⁣
It was at a kut ceremony/ritual when grandpa saw grandma, he must of fell head over heels for her. Soon he left the monkhood, and ran over to grandma to be happily married. Heheh. ⁣
⁣
Now, they're  a 굿 kut performing duo. I've listened and heard alot of drumming types and styles....but in my eyes, no one comes close to my spirits grandfather. I miss his sounds, his rhythm and strength when he plays for the spirits. ⁣
⁣
My time with my elders, my spirit grandparents taught me alot as I listened to their stories. How spirit grandmother was chosen to be a mudang, her struggles, faults and mistakes. I listened to every detail, taking in all the knowledge and life wisdom she had to share. ⁣
⁣
Its these intimate moments, we learn and grow. Listening to the stories of our people, culture and ancestors. ⁣
⁣

posts.caption:
Mudangs purchase their altar/shrine items from a mudang supply store.  Basic altar items like the water offering bowls, liquor offerings cups, incense holder and altar candle holders are needed when setting up an altar. ⁣ ⁣When the mudang is initiated,  and ready to serve her gods through her own 신당,  2 rituals are performed. First would be the blessing and clearing, it's also a ritual that seeks to harmonize with the local land deity of the home. Its known as a 고사, requiring the traditional offerings within the many parts of the home. Along with a bowl of red bean porridge as it chases and clear any negative spirits. ⁣
The 2nd ceremony/ritual will be the drumming, with the chants/prayers of the mudang. Calling down the gods to be seated within their shrine embodied through murals, folk paintings, calligraphy words, tools associated with the gods, etc. ⁣
When a mudang have to shut her 산당 for whatever reason, no longer serving the gods through a shrine. Then another ceremony/ritual must done to "unseat" the gods, ancestral spirits and deities. It's important to do so, especially after the gods were called down, its proper to send them off. ⁣
What happens to the altar items then? They must be handle with great care and respect, either given back to a mudang store willing to take it. Or take it to a mudang prayer and 굿 camp lodges where they use the items for the many altars. ⁣If the mudang has statues of the gods those cant be discarded improperly, can be given to a Buddhist temple in Korea where they serve them. There has been horror stories of people improperly discarding holy sacred items, with the spirits retaliating.

We first open the 굿 invoking the gods, each called down, giving 공수 (channelled divination) to the guests. ⁣
⁣
When 볼살 (Bulsa) grandmother goddess is called, she opens the door to grab one of the ancestral spirit of whom the 굿 is for.⁣
⁣
It's when 대신 (Daesin) Grandmother goddess is invoked that she opens the doors, its through her connection we allow the ancestors spirits to come. ⁣
⁣
Every god/deity is different for every mudang. Two mudangs can have 산신 in their pantheon, but the 산신's will be different. Due to the different ancestors deified to be 산신, and the many different inter positions within a 산신. ⁣
⁣
Not all mudangs have the ability to fully embody, be completely taken over and possessed by an ancestor spirit. It's an innate gift the shaman must be born with, also requiring a very specific 대신 Grandmother Goddess,  since there many types of 대신 roles. ⁣

posts.caption:
Few years back, the drums came for me. 
I was always anxious, I couldnt sleep, I couldnt eat, I wasnt comfortable at all.

At night, visions would terrify me leaving me petrified. I would see the shadows move about in the room. 
In the shower as I wiped the water off my face, my eyes went blank, my vision blurred,  grayed and blacked out. I couldnt see for a few seconds but it felt like forever. I freaked out, screamed, and yelled for my husband. He went with me everywhere,  to the bathroom when I need to pee and shower. He was always there to be my human shield, my knight. 
I could hear the drums banging, and it would only start at night. When I closed my eyes, the drums sounded louder, making me miserable. The sounds of the  drums was accompanied by the intense desire to run into the woods, the forest. Over time, I felt trapped and had thoughts of abandoning my family to run into the mountains. 
I grew severely depressed, and sleep deprived due to the endless 가위눌려, 'sleep paralysis '. Not to mention the chronic pain, the multiple surgeries I've gone through. 
I went to many healers, psychics, witches, mediums, and shamans. I was told that I had a curse done on my family, from my mother's side. Not one was able to help me, and I'm convinced some of them made it worse for me...messing with something they shouldnt of. 
Now, I look at all my horrific past experiences and I understand now.  There's a saying in Korean "그릇을 만들어"...means to make a bowl/dish. It refers to the process of shaping, pounding and working with clay to make the dish/bowl you need. ⁣
⁣
⁣
My gods shaped and molded to be the "bowl" they needed me to be. 🍵

Today is Buddhas birthday known as the "Day Buddha Arrived " in Korea. This morning we set the altar with all the offerings. On this day, traditionally we eat a vegetarian bibimbap with barley rice. 
Spirit mom drummed, sanged and banged her mokugyo performing ceremonial rites for Buddhas birthday. 
Early afternoon we finished the ceremony,  my sisters and I cleared everything away. Since we were all just chatting away, spirit mom took out the delicate colored papers so we can fold, while we chatted. 
These paper flowers are offerings we make at every kut ritual, these flowers will be put on the altar meant for the ancestors during the kut ceremony. 
The flower serves a roles as a tangible offering to show the spirits dedication and devotion. The origins of the paper flower started when flowers were incredibly hard to come by during cold wintery months.
These paper flower also play a huge role within the Korean Buddhist as well, used for many rites and ceremonies. 
We have several kut ceremony/ritual happening back to back, grateful for the opportunity to learn and grow as a mudang.

posts.caption:
Yakgwa (약과) is up on my altar from this past new moon offerings. ⁣
⁣
It's a traditional Korean cookie, usually with a flower shape being pressed into wooden molds and some times decorated with nuts and/or dates. Yakgwa literal translation is "medicinal confection", as 'yak' means medicine and 'gwa' means cookie or fruit. The medicinal part refers to the large amounts of honey used in it. ⁣
⁣
They were mainly used as offerings for ancestral rites, court banquets, holidays and special celebrations. ⁣
⁣
This snack has one of the longest history  within the Korean cuisine, ⁣originating during the Three Kingdoms era. People would use powered grains mixed with other ingredients, to shape them into fruit or flower shapes when they couldnt find any actually fruits to use during ancestral rites, court banquets, ceremonies and rituals. ⁣
Due to their usage for rituals, its gained popularity and became the must-have food for those occasions. So popular that they had shortages of its main ingredient such as flour, honey, etc.⁣
⁣
Ancient kings of Goryeo even banned people from making of the yakgwa. ⁣
In modern Joseon era, these snacks were mostly enjoyed by the upper Yangban social class. Wheat, honey, and other scarce precious ingredients were highly regarded. ⁣
⁣

I realized that I should talk about the different ways, a mudang have her spirits, embodies them. Many multiple ways of having a shrine room, and I will discuss the differences of each. Hope everyone is doing great.

I am grateful for everyone who I connect with, as they too also help me heal and further on in my path.

posts.caption:
Alot of times we are tested, our beliefs and faith are tested by the gods and deities. They watch carefully how we act and react, constantly throwing obstacles at us to see how we prevail. 
I know, and I can feel what my spirits expectations of me are, as well as mine. It when times are tough, that our faith and beliefs are tested even more. The polishing of one's rock. Just like how the waters will polish a rock smooth, not with brute force but with time, patience and gentleness. Being a shaman isnt about rushing through our journey, its being mindful of the path we walk.
A while ago, I decided to pray, meditate and be in the moment in my shrine room [신당]. My gods and spirits told me that I should not be running and scramble up the mountain, because I might overlook many things. Instead my spirits told me to take one step at a time,  and look around, take in what I see and feel. To enjoy the moment and be aware of the moment, regardless if it's good or bad. My spirits said this is not a race, and not about being in first place. Its about who "dish" is deeper, and holds more water. 
In Korea, we have a saying that not every dish (person) is the same, some are short, shallow, big or deep. My spirits said I must shape my dish slowly, and I must strive to be a dish that's very deep. Deep so that I may hold alot of water, and give back alot of water. [This picture is taken at the mountain top of Ohdaesan, a temple resides. Within these walls, lies the remains of Buddha so it says.]
In times of hardship,  I look to my ancestral spirits, my gods and deities for guidance. posts.caption:
What's the etiquette of visiting a mudangs shrine/temple?⁣ Alot of people ask me, what is the proper way and behavior of the sindang [신당] shrine/temple. Many arent accustomed to the traditions. At one point, I too, didnt know what the proper etiquettes were but I will share what I know. ⁣
☆Entering the shrine room, you may light an incense if you desire to. Proper respects is to bow, in a sets of 3 or 9 full body bows. If bowing is difficult, then bow your head with your hands together in the prayer form.⁣
☆Never have your back turned towards the altar, the gods are facing towards you, so be mindful not to show your back. ⁣
☆Sitting on the floor in the shrine room [traditional style] on floor cushions, for some it may be difficult. You can stretch your legs out but dont point your feet towards the altar. ⁣
☆No cursing, be mindful of the language used.⁣
☆Set your offerings on the altar whether its payment for a reading or other types of offerings. ⁣
What can you bring as an offering?⁣
Fruit (no stone fruit), liquor (*no makkoli rice wine), cakes, rice cakes, cookie, candy, pastry goods, rice or money. Offerings must be new, purchased with the intentions to use as offerings. Not something laying around in your pantry/fridge. ⁣
• Makkoli rice wine [막걸리] is an offering usually given to the low end spirits so cant be used as an offering to the gods. ⁣
⁣
📷 taken in Korea, on our way to visit the waterfall of the 9 Generals. ⁣

posts.caption:
How long does it take to train as a mudang [korean shaman]. Most mudangs takes about 3 years or so to learn the way of our spirits. Traditional, when one finds the appropriate lineage and teacher, the mudang-to-be would enter their elders home. Help in the day to day life of their elder, shadowing their every move. Even doing mundane tasks of helping her spirit mother clean their home, cook, and run daily errands. This is true especially for the low hierarchy apprentice, who needs to work their way up in the skills. 
Most Korean mudangs here in the US, dont have the basic training. Usually going to Korea to get their initiation,  unable to commit to shadowing their spirit mother, without any training or guidance. This I feel can be a very slippery slope, as most wouldnt know how to proceed with shrine care duties of their temple,  setting up of offerings, aiding clients with rituals and ceremonies. To me this is very worrisome,  as the newbie mudangs are left unguided. Its imperative that the newbie mudangs keeps in constant contact with their elder, to learn, grow and to discuss. 
It's like as if someone who graduated to be a doctor but never step foot in a hospital or a clinic, how would they know to provide patient care. 
One thing I find to struggle with, is when in prayer our spirits communicate. Sometimes we may think the spirits is telling us something,  when in fact it's hard to decipher if its really the case due to our desire and wants. 
In my case, since I am searching for a new apartment.  I ask my spirits if this place is good to be seated, they say yes because I really loved the newly renovated place. But bring my spirit mother over to take a look, she disproves because the energy of the land, the spirits of this home is too chaotic, which can interfere with my work. Dismiss a teacher lead to chaos. 
On our way Ilwolsan, I stopped to prayed briefly at the altar of the fairy maiden Sonyeo. 선녀

posts.caption:
Todays ancestors offering table, for the kut 굿 ceremony/ritual.  What an auspicious day to perform a ceremony for the client which is the brother of my spirit sister. Today is a full moon, known as 보름, [boreum], it's a 굿 ceremony which we ask for blessings and guidance from the spirits to help out the clients family. 
Spirit mom drum in the main shrine room, calling the gods and deities one by one, singing our prayers. We then move into the room with the ancestral offerings, drumming there to call down the ancestors,  singing our prayers wishing the ancestors peace and harmony. 
When we were doing the 대수대명 [Daesu-Daemyoung] the effergy dolls, wrapping in the undergarments of each family member.  I was overcomed by a series of nonstop yawning. Happens everytime, each time I assist with the dolls for every 굿 ritual.  Spirit mom tells me its because the spirits are entering me, I'm affected by their presence. 
Some mudangs would start yawning out of nowhere,  or even start whistling about.  All indications of spirits. Please dont misunderstand, while its possible for laypeople to yawn and whistle, it must be during a kut ritual or at the shrine. I don't mean that everything we yawn a spirit enters, it depends on the situation and we are doing at hand.

posts.caption:
It's only been a few months since I came back from Korea, and already my soul longs for the craggy rocky peaks of its glorious mountains. The sounds of the drums and gongs calling me back home to the land where my gods and ancestors were birthed. 
The energy of the sacred places, filled with  the lively energy of my spirits. My heart yearns for the simple things, and the deep lessons given to me while touring the sacred shrines. 
Just looking into the sky, you can feel it explode with energy. Having my first initiation almost 3 years ago, I can feel the beats of the drums, the words of our sacred songs. Its pull, calling me over and over. 
This coming year, I dont know if I can go back due to logistics. But I hope that my spirits can open up the doorways and path that will allow me to somehow step foot on its soil. I am a diaspora, born and raised in a foreign land. My parents immigrated to give me a better life, while I am forever grateful for that opportunity, I still long for my ancestral land. Its also because of that disconnect, I am more determined to continue on my elders lineage and legacy of following the traditions despite the ever changing modern influence. While everyone is striving for a convenient lifestyle due to the bounties of modern efficiency. I want to hold onto the sacred rites, and traditions of my Korean heritage. Its becoming more watered down, and the basic etiquettes of ancestral worship and spiritual worship is overlooked. 
My elder couldnt believed how sacred shrine and prayer sites no longer had mudangs bustling about. posts.caption:
What's the shamanic aspect of mental illness like bipolar disorder, or multiple personality and schizophrenia. What's the shamanic aspect of hiccups? 
I constantly get messages about people asking me about my perspective on their mental illness and instability. I am NOT a doctor, I cannot replace what doctors, therapy and other treatments can do for mental illness. 
Yes, sometimes there can be a reason why a person's mental state can be spiritual influenced but that does not mean its every case. Please seek out medical attention. With spiritual arts exploding in popularity with reiki, witches, shamans and other spiritual paths, there are many articles how mental illness is treated by spiritual leaders. I cannot say how dangerous that is as a shaman myself. It's best to go seek a doctor, especially in cases when people are severely ill. 
Yes, in some cases working with a shaman can help but that isnt every case. Just like taking vitamin supplements helps a person immune system or help with their calcium,  it does not replace doctors. 
Working with the gods, deities and spirits means to work in conjunction,  working together while receiving aid/treatment from doctors medically. 
I've seen and witnessed firsthand how powerful my shamanic lineage can be with  successful outcomes of a kut 굿 ceremony/ritual but I would never ever advise anyone to dismiss their doctors. 
Please if you suspect anyone is suffering,  do not it go untreated. Please find a proper doctor with merit, and seek professional advice and diagnosis.
Working together in conjunction I believes provides the best outcome helping fill in the gaps. 
NO shaman can help cure your dental issue, if your teeth is rotting away. No amount of drumming and ritual ceremony can help restore your tooth, or your heart. It doesnt work in that sense. So please seek out medical treatment.

posts.caption:
@merlegeode ask me share my story behind my logo. Ask what is my story, and how I came to choose this. 
The 5 colors of red, blue, white, yellow and green represents the colors on the Korean shaman culture. Each colors has various meanings, representing the 5 directions, seasons, and also indication of the gods and deities. These same colors are deeply rooted in the culture, on clothing, food and architecture influencing the Korean lifestyle. 
I chosed to have it be represented in the form of the Rose of Sharon, the national flower of Korea known as 무궁화 [Mugunghwa] a flower that symbolized the independence of Korea. Mugung means everlasting or immortal, and hwa meaning flower. The five petals also represents the 5 traditional types of happiness, duty unity all translating to the peace and happiness. There's even a song we sing dedicated to the flower "Mugunghwa, Mugunghwa our flower of the nation/ land". The Sam-Taeguk (tricolor)symbol of the red, yellow and blue used in Korean shamanism represents Cheon-Ji-In, which means Heaven, Earth and Humanity going back to the Joseon period. Widely used everywhere in the Korean culture. 
I wanted the symbols with deep historical meanings to come together in the form of a simple mandala. Bringing me back to the beginnings of my spiritual journey, where I would sit under trees meditating and drawing mandalas. 
In a way, my logo, my personal symbol tells the story of my path, my growth. And it all came to me in a vision. 
Thank you for allowing me to share, and many thanks to Merle, for suggesting this. Please ask me, anything you would like for me to share/discuss as I'm bursting with stories to tell. 😁

posts.caption:
Jowangsin [조왕신] the goddess of the kitchen hearth and fire. This shamanic deity has long been revered by housewives since the early 3rd century.Jowangsin is a gasin, a branch of deities that protects the home.  The goddess is personified into an offering bowl of water perched on an altar above the hearth. Offerings of fresh new water must be given daily, with a prayer. On special occasion, rice cakes, fruits, with rice and other offerings are set on a table for the deity. The kitchen served as a symbol of good fortune, a good fire indicated wealth. The goddess also serves a role as a scribe, writing down and recording all the daily happenings of the home and family, reporting it to the Heavens. 
Jowangsin deity has 5 rules one must follow when in her kitchen perimeter. (1) No cursing (2) Do not put your feet up on her hearth (3) Dont sit on her hearth (4) Maintain a clean kitchen (5) You may worship other kitchen deities. 
Due to the status of Jowangsin as gasin, she is a lowly deity compared to the Heavenly deities like Chilseong or Sansin. She is not a deity that is presented in an illustrated form like the other gods, though her role is important within the household. 
Jowangsin is most indefinitely a goddess, but the few images available online interestingly, depicts a male. The kitchen god, is also a deity that is widely worshipped in China, and is portrayed as a male. Some korean Buddhist temples have an altar with an male image of Jowangsin. Alot of shamanic deities, roots and myths have been rewritten to serve the Buddhist views. In my opinion, there are misgnonism aspects of Buddhism being a patriarchal system side weeping the matriarchs of Korean shamans.
I dont have a personal altar for Jowangsin within my home, but on many important holidays I do set up grand offerings in my kitchen, paying my respects to Jowangsin.
Jowangsin was rivals with the toilet goddess Cheukshin. * Not my images.

Chilseong [칠성], the "Seven Star" shamanic deity of the Big Dipper constellation. It is said, in the Korean night sky, the big dipper constellation stars shined the brightest. The chilseong worship is one of the oldest within the shamanic culture, revered by woman for their family households and by mudang [shamans]. [Chilseong] is thought to be the protector of the Korean people.  Governing the lifeline longevity of the people, health, peace and most importantly, the health and life span of children. Until a child is 7 years old, their health and life line is under the care of Samsin, but afterwards, it is looked after by Chilseong under their care.
Chilseong is a Heavenly deity, usually depicted as 7 men but idolized as one shamanic deity. Among the 7 stars, there is usually a leader, the one who holds the book of consciousness. 
At the time of Buddhist introduction, the two most prominent shamanic god/deities were Sanshin [god of mountain/earth] and Chilseong. It was important for Buddhism to absorb these two shamanic deities, as they help give rise to the Buddhist and Taoist movement. 
Spirit mom told me monks were first wandering peddlers that people ignored, their beliefs and teachings wasnt accepted. It was the mudangs who helped clothe and feed the starving monks. They in return used our gods for their advantage.
Every year there is a day dedicated to Chilseong,  offerings tables are set and the names of children are written on long white cloth to ask for their blessings and protection. This year I will have both my boys participate in the ritual to have the names written in the stars, asking for Chilseong' grace

posts.caption:
Samsin [삼신], the grandmother deity known as the goddess of children and/or childbearing. She is a shamanic deity and a house spirit that watches, protects and guides all children until the age of 7 years. 
Most household have a "danji" [earthen pot deity shrine] within the "warmest part of the home" as the location of Samsin.  When a child is born, it is customary to set up an offering table of seaweed soup [miyuk gook], steamed rice, water, and 3 vegetable sides. When the child hits various milestones like 100th day and 1 year birthday, an offering table is set for Samsin to give gratitude and ask for blessings. "Sam" [pronounced sahm] means three, "Sin" [pronounced shin] means god or deity. Samsin is a triple goddess treated as one deity. She is also a household deity [gasin] protecting the inner quarters of the home. Samsin is also know as Jesuk or Jesok, depicted as the 3 Buddhist. 
All children enter this world upon with the blessing of Samsin, but their fate lifeline is determined by  Chilseong, the deity of the seven stars [big dipper constellation]
With the introduction of buddhism in the early 4th century, most shamanic origin myth and stories were re-written with the influence of the Male monks. Samsin is originally 3 goddess but rewritten as 3 Male bodhisattva of fate, luck and mercy. posts.caption:
Peach Blossoms. 🍑
Peaches are usually a sign, a symbol for the spring season. Most people think of the peach, as a sign of good luck, fortune and longevity. 
But the peach [the fruit and the tree] has another role within the Korean shaman customs. It is use to drive out spirits, ghosts, negativity and exorcism. Since peach represents spring of the yang [energy], it is most effective tool against warding off negative spirits. 
This is why peaches are NEVER ever put on the offering tables for the ancestors [jesa] and for the gods/deities. 
Peaches are also in fact, a fruit that is depicted within murals and paintings of the gods/deities. The fruit of the spirits, represents good luck and fortune, but the fruit shown in the paintings are not the same "type". These are the heavenly peaches growing within the heavenly realms of the gods and deities, so it's not same "peach" as the one grown on this earthly plane. 
The peach has a long history within the shamanic rituals of the mudangs, that it is even revered in the shaman songs called muga. 
So when setting up any offering table to ancestors or spirits, please be mindful not to put any peaches or other stone fruits like plums, nectarines, apricots, cherries, etc.

posts.caption:
Happy full moon, the Great Moon festival. 
It's known as 대보름 [Dae Bo-reum], the festival of the 'Great Full Moon' and the 1st full moon of the new Lunar Year. 
It's an auspicious day, and traditionally sacrifices were made to the Heavens in offerings, or lighting of the lanterns. 
There are so many traditions in respect to this full moon. Some traditions are cracking walnuts with teeth, or climbing the mountain to witness the 1st sun rise, or stealing mud from wealthy homes, etc. 
The main custom is to eat 오곡밤 [O-go-bap] which is rice mixed with other grains and various beans, along with side dishes of only vegetables namuls and nuts. This customary meal helped people replenish nutrients that was lost during the cold winter months when food was scarce. 
There are many celebrated folk traditions and customs associated with this day. One the folk games villagers and children would play was the game of tug-of- war. 
Mask dances served as exorcism to expel evil and bring good fortune to the villagers. 
I wish everyone a very prosperous Lunar Year. I hope everyone had a great first Lunar full moon.

posts.caption:
"Once you carry your own water, you value each drop" - Author Unknown .
.
This echoes the same sentiments I try to express when I try to explain the very simple act of water offerings. 
A teacher took on a young apprentice, and one of the first tasks to learn, was to fetch the teacher a bowl of water everyday. Each day when the apprentice gave her a bowl of water, the teacher spilled it out. Every morning after morning,  the same thing happened. The apprentice tried to figure out what she did wrong, so she ask if the teacher wanted warm water, or cold water, room temperature, or flavored water. Each time she asked a question, the teacher just replied to bring a bowl of water. Months went by, and finally the apprentice had a tantrum fit, crying about. 
The teacher sternly told her, if you cant complete a simple task as fetching a bowl of water, then you dont deserve to learn under me. The basics of your foundation must be strong, and yet you fail at bringing a bowl of water. 
The apprentice picked up the bowl, and every morning she continued and each time the teacher spilled it out. Then one day, the apprentice took her time and pondered about the water. This time, she thoughtfully boiled the water with ginger, cooled it down and brought it to her teacher. This time it wasnt spilled out, and instead the teacher asked to explain.
The apprentice said, she realized the task wasnt about the water at all. It was never ever about the water.  It was about the heart and the emotion she carried while performing the task of fetching the water.
.
It's this deep meaningful message I hope to teach to my spirit sisters and my clients. One of the first things we do, is pour water offerings. Of course we pour fresh new water, but it isnt about the water. Instead it's about our hearts and mind while performing these tasks. The ability to look deeper in, the understanding of respect and mindfulness. Todays kut ceremony/ritual is a 재수굿 [jesu kut], a ritual to bring in more luck, blessings and prosperity abundance. The clients are Russian, operating a construction business in Brooklyn. 
Their 1st ceremony was last year, a sickness ceremony for their young daughter who has a medical condition of constantly falling asleep.

Because it is a jesu kut, we will be using a whole pig offering to Daegam [대감]. When raising of the pig, if it stands quickly it means that things will work out quickly. If the pig sway back and forth a bit and then stand, means it will take some time to find stability but in the end, things will work out. Based on how the pig stands, foretells us by the Daegam deityhow soon or quickly,  luck will find them.

She is the rainbow in my sky, and I am just here to learn from her. I am so honored to have met someone who I look up to with such sacred honor, that is why she is my teacher, my spirit mother.

Todays kut ceremony/ritual is for a client living in Japan. A korean man living in Japan for some time, desiring to make it his home. For reasons, he has no luck in anything. Hard to find a job, housing, nothing ever works out for him and he is always teetering tottering unable to find some stability. 
Todays kut is a 재수 굿, a ceremony/ritual to bring in more luck, blessings into ones life. Asking the gods [신] to blow in the winds of a prosperous change. 
When we grabbed the ancestors, his family is from the Jeollado province. His grandfather passed early because he was beaten and tortured by the Japanese during the occupation.  He told us how he was a farmer and that the Japanese demanded most of their goods leaving the farmers with scraps for food. When the quota is met, he said they gather everyone from the village to torture and beat them. 
Then grandpa said , I passed away getting beat by the Japanese and my grandson is over there trying to settle down, what a destiny. We all laughed at his remark, and sent him along the way to the spirit world with new clothes, money after he had his fill of food and liquor. 
This post isnt about being anti Japanese or anything negative about Japan.  This is about releasing and healing the pain of our ancestors, the spirits of our blood and bone.

The first thing he said to me, that "since hes been born he's only caused his parents deep grief. Its because of me, my parents lost their lands."
He felt guilty despite it was his family who schemed for his fathers land. He told me he still visit his ancestral burial sites, and he was heartbroken when there was overgrown grass and branches scattered because it was unattended to, forgotten. 
I told him, Grandpa please do not fill your heart with han, let it be like the waters of the river and release. There isnt much left of your lifeline, please dont spend it in agony & anger. Keep your soul/heart in good health so that when you journey back to the spirit world, you can properly pay your respects to your ancestors spirits, your parents. He broke his somber with laughter, asked me if I really believe if he would meet his parents again. I said, I wholeheartedly would pray that he does, and I know he will as long as he doesnt harbors ANY han. I told him, grandpa I dont want you wandering on this plane, your spirit stuck here cold and hungry because your han prevented your passage. I said, not even your kids will perform a jesa table for you in your honor. Please find your peace. 
We spoke of lost traditions and the respect of the ancestors. When a person passed away, an offering [jesa] table was prepared every single day for 3 years. 
He told me he know his sons will do nothing for him in his honor. He wanted to tell his older son that he doesnt even expect a jesa offering table, he just wants to be visited and his burial place cared for. 
I went shopping earlier and oddly, I picked up two pairs of gloves. When I looked at his hands cold and weathered from the frigid air, I quickly gave him warm new gloves. I whispered to myself, I wondered why I bought 2 gloves, and now I know. I put a pack of soft tissues in his pocket and tried to convince him to allow me to give him a drive as he refused. I ushered him down the stairs and turned to bow at me, and I bowed back.

[Part 1/2]
Had a client today, it was an elderly man with a hearing problem. 
Helped him into my shrine room, and he came with a stack of papers. He sat down and told me he was so fustrated, he didn't have a person to speak with so, he came to me to find some peace.  Born in 1937, when Korea was still under Japanese occupation. He said most of his life, for his meals all he grew up with was a side of [gochujang] and cabbage kimchi. White rice was a precious grain, and it was a seasonal food they rarely had on their table. 
He also told me that he entered school in the first grade at 10 yrs old. In school, there were many ranges of kids from 8 to 16 years old, attending the first grade. Mostly education was invested in boys, as the girls stayed home and learned how to run the household and kitchens. 
While serving the military , his father passed away in an accident. Although the family was poor, they had a few parcels of land. He was so busy with working and providing for his family,  that he never thought about the land until many, many years later. He was able to sell one land piece for 2 sacks of rice, and other land he had no idea what happened. 
He told me that he went to Korea 2 years ago to visit the burial of his parents, he was heartbroken that their gravesite wasnt managed or maintained, it pained him dearly. 
He was furious at his uncles, because he suspected it was them who deceived his mother and sold off his fathers land without seeing a nickel from it. He was upset, sad and filled with han. He humbly put his hands together and bowed before my gods enshrined in my thankka. He asked for the answers, I relayed the messages from my spirits and he sat still and listened. His back was curved, shoulders drooped and hung his head low as I felt his injustice.

posts.caption:
Today is the full moon,  and we are in the sindang [temple/shrine room] of my beloved spirit mother. We are gathered here to perform a special kut ceremony/ritual, a 49th day ritual. 
The clients father in law recently departed from this world, and to help him transition peacefully and harmonious,  we held a kut in his honor and of his ancestral spirits. 
For a ritual like this, we set up a special table with rice formed into a shape of a person. We take offerings that will be given to the spirit and lay it over the table with special ritual coverings making sure the figure isnt disturbed. 
We call the spirits of the clients, their ancestors one by one including her father in law. We gift them food, liquor and clothing to wear from the offering table. Each ancestor comes and spend their time speaking of their stories of grief or happiness, as they release their traumas through storytelling. 
After all the spirits are sent away, and the ritual has come to a close. We remove the rice figure coverings and a new shape or imprint will form. Giving us insight to the new form the ancestor spirit has taken like a bird, dog, wolf, bear, etc. This is the new form the spirit has taken in on their travel back to the heavenly world of our ancestors. 
I hope that when I return back to my spirits and ancestors,  I can do so with integrity, dignity and honor. I hope they I did my ancestors proud with my work here.

Beoseon [버선] 
When I toured Korea, my heart fluttered everytime I saw these. The traditional socks of Korea, shows the sorrows and joys of our Korean mothers and grandmothers. How you ask?
In traditional times, during holidays mothers and grandmothers would hand sew all the new clothing for their families to wear, such as new year. The woman would stay up all night long sewing and sewing tirelessly, so she may clothe her family in new garments.  When I first saw these at the marketplace,  I thought of my grandmother and it raised alot of bittersweet emotions. 
Even mudangs to this day, still wear beoseon's during kut ceremony/ritual. I sometimes do wear these beoseon myself. In older days when mudangs jumped during ceremonies,  they use to pour water on the wooden floors so the mudang wouldnt slip with the beoseon. The socks are slippery and throwing water down gave it grip. 
Growing up in NYC, I never thought of my ancestors,  my culture or traditions at all. And now, all I do is think of different ways of preserving what is sacred. Maybe because my ancestors are with me, I feel a stronger sense to protect these sacred traditions. Times are evolving and many are choosing modernism over traditions,  including mudangs. I choose to preserve my traditions, because I want to keep on weaving the story of our ancestors joy, sorrows and pains. I feel that keeping with my culture and traditions, is the physical storytelling of our ancestors. Someone told me that traditions like a fire that we keep adding wood to, to keep it alive. Beautiful indeed.

posts.caption:
Korea has long been a shamanic country, every person had multiple shrines and altar with a danji within their homes.  A danji is earthenware jar that enshrines a sacred deity that is worshipped. Just a few decades ago, people still had a separate shrine room to serve their ancestral spirits performing jaesa and other duties to their spirits. Koreans are very spirited people and nation. 
Even common folks knew how to perform basic shamanic rituals without the aid of a mudang. The village mudang will teach others  to perform simple cleansing and exorcism rituals to maintain peace and harmony within the household. Some even had fortune telling intuition but that still wasnt enough to be marked as a mudang. 
Nowadays there is a huge spiritual movement, I get many inquiries from alot of people. Being a mudang is not the only path in my shamanic culture. If one feels compelled to serve the spirits, its usually our ancestors. They are our anchors, and our axis that serves to connect our spirited realm of the gods and deities. Some are inevitably marked and chosen by the spirits, but there is 2 types of markings. 
It makes me happy to know many are seeking the path to become more spirited like our ancestors before. It was the way of life to respect nature, to pay our respects to the natural world.

Happy Full Moon everyone and an amazing Winter Solstice. 
Normally for the full moon, I prepare offerings on a minor scale compared to my New Moon offerings. But nonetheless,  offerings are made daily despite it being a new moon or full moon. 
Its also winter solstice,  and traditionally in my korean culture we eat 'ppat juk' which is red bean porridge. The red bean porridge is actually an offering that is made because it acts like an exorcism of cleansing bad energy and spirits. Its used to chase away ghosts and other spirit beings. Usually people will gather in their homes to perform ancestral rites before eating their porridge, and they also put out a bowl of porridge put into every room to ward off the negative spirits. Nowdays this practice is not done by today's Koreans. 
But I am ironically very traditional despite my upbringing. I will provide red bean porridge as my offerings, and perform a cleansing rite and putting porridge in every room of my house to cleanse and purify. Have an amazing winter solstice and a beautiful full moon everyone.

posts.caption:
MU•DANG
What does it mean? Why do I use this term to call myself as opposed to a MAN•SHIN. 
The word itself is a term with great respect. 
MU means spirits, the shaman. DANG means an altar [in simple terms]. Some say this part refers to Dangun the founder of Korea, the grandson of the Heavenly King and of the motherly Bear. 
MUDANG means a living altar for the spirits,  for the gods [신] it is the epitome of what it means to be a shaman. A sacrificial lamb of sorts, I am the sacrifice,  the living altar for my spirits. A life path dedicated to my spirits,  whom I serve with every step, every breath. 
I dont choose to call myself a Manshin meaning [ten thousand spirits], I reserve that term for my elders, the veteran mudangs. How does one become a manshin? In my humble opinion,  a mudang becomes a manshin by having multiple initiations. Its during this initiations [맞이굿] that that different gods enter and leave the pantheon of the mudang. In time, the spirits the mudang encounters will be ten thousand, therefore being called a Manshin. 
Most Korean shamans, dont call themselves mudang because of the negativity that surrounds it. But I embrace it, despite what others may do because the title reminds me of the burden I must carry, the weight of my ancestors. My path isnt laid out with the red carpet, the insights and the deep lessons I learned is from falling many times. From learning under the wing and the guidance of my amazing spirit mother.
🙏

I wanted to make sure that when the spirit of my grandmother comes,  she can at the very least 'peel a layer' of her 'han', suffering and anguish. I wanted to make sure that despite the toxic and abusive relationship she and I had, that may find the peace she needs. 
When I first realized I had to do a ceremony/ritual for my grandmother,  I was angry. I was very upset, and angry that the responsibility fell on my shoulders. Out of all the people she could of gone to [her 7 children], she came to me. My grandmother was not a nice person, most of my trauma stemmed from her. So I felt anger, and felt it was unfair to me......
But then I remembered my vision,  and the message my 신 [gods] told me to keep the waters of my heart pure and untainted. So that I would have the merit and ability to serve my spirits and carry my gods. I made peace with my past, and accepted this weight that I must carry. This is afterall what the burden of a mudang is, to have to carry on the weight of it all and then some.

This Tues I have my own kut ceremony/ritual that I must do for my ancestors. My grandmother passed sometime in October,  and as a mudang I should never attend funerals. In addition,  the news of someone's passing should not be told to me or ever enter my ears either. Why? Because of the spirits,  and the negative influence/affect of the recently passed spirit which we call Samu ssal. 
A properly initiated mudang, or even an experienced veteran mudang cannot withstand the winds of Samu-ssal. The bad luck and energy of a persons passing can affect us, negatively. Performing an exorcism can help, but still wont be able to fully neutralize the negativity of Samu ssal. 
Traditionally,  when a person passes away they are given 49 days to 'wander around' and tie up loose ends, seeking their closure. When the 영 'young' [soul/spirit] has alot of anger and trauma which we refer to as 한 'han'...that spirit wont be able to pass into the spirit world peacefully. 
My grandmother was someone who was chosen and marked by the spirits, but she was unable to fulfill her destiny as a mudang. Instead she walked in the path of the Catholic faith, and despite being chosen by the gods... she began to mix the two up, and forming her own unique twist.

posts.caption:
(Part 2/2)
My culture we had a social class system, the noble ruling class of aristocrats Yangban. The lowest  is the Cheonmin, and it was mainly due the professions that were seen as 'unclean' like butchers, metalworkers, the shoemakers, kiaseng and mudangs, etc. 
A mudang will train a entire lifetime, and when one fails at being a shaman....we became kiaseng,  entertainers of the ruling yangban class. A mudang is an entertainer of the gods, the spirits. To be an initiated mudang, or marked by the spirits does not guarantee immediate success. One must know how to dance gracefully, seamlessly in between the thin veil between the living and the spirits. 
Spirit mother shook her head in disbelief how the many mudang [shamans] act like they are above others, showing off lavish lifestyles and prancing about. She looked at me, and told me to never forget why we became a mudang, why we are chosen. 
A mudang means a lifetime of service, lifetime of struggles, of many sufferings and hardships. Why? Why is that? 
Its to repent, its karma, to make up for the many lifetimes of sin, and bad karma we committed collectively. That process of 'polishing our rock', she told me to polish, and polish, and polish....a lifetime of polishing for our ancestors, our karma and our future children. The more we 'polish' the more our gods, our spirits,  our ancestors can rise from the chains of their own karma. This is why we are working a lifetime of service, of prayers for ourselves and our seekers. We carry the karma and the weight of our clients, we build up ourselves so we can serve the gods and mankind. 
This is truly a heavy weight to carry, when a mudang commits a sin...it is a strike against our gods and ancestors, and ourselves. When we commit harmful acts, we prevent the path of our spirits...and therefore preventing our own, cutting off our own lifeline. 
This is a deep lesson that always stays with me, and constantly echos. When my time comes to meet my gods in the spirit world, I truly hope I can stand tall with honor and integrity.

posts.caption:
My daily ritual for my sindang (신당), my temple, altar and sacred space. 
Most are curious about my daily life, my daily rituals for my altar and sacred space. 
I try to do most of my daily rituals in the morning, but sometimes its difficult with 2 rambunctious boys, 3 boys (if you include my hubs). Before walking into temple, its seen as proper to wash up and enter the sacred space with a clean body. A sacred space must be entered with pure mind, heart and body, this is where my spirits, my gods and ancestors are venerated, so I want to be always mindful. 
I empty my water offering bowls, and fetch new clean water from the sink. I have a water pot specifically for my temple only, its purpose is for water offerings only. I do not mix any of my personal items with the items of the spirits, including bowls, plates or whatever I use in my temple. 
Candles are lit, and water offerings is given to the middle first, the left second, the right third and to my house guardian out in my foyer lastly. Next up is my liquor offerings done in the same respect and manner. 
Last part is when I light an incense,  which I light from the candle. I never ever blow out the flame that lit the incense, and instead I shake it gently between two hands to snuff out the flame. Everything must be done in a mindful manner. The offerings we give is important, but its even more important - to be mindful of the offerings we give to the gods, of our hearts and mind when performing these daily ritual. Fetching water and pouring the water offerings is not what this lesson is about....anyone can fetch and pour water. Its about the openness, the depth of our gratitude in our hearts and mind, while we pour the water and other offerings.

posts.caption:
In the sacred shamanic mountains of Ilwolsan, named after the 'Sun-moon' connection and its deep sacred shamanic roots. This mountain is also known for its haunted peak, roamed by a particular ghost or spirit. 
In one of the shrines, prayer temples we visited is a small wooden structure dedicated to Hawng-ssi-buin 황씨 부인 [means Mr. Hwangs wife]. The legend goes to say, that Mrs. Hwang ran away from the terrible abuse of her mother in law, and ended up committing suicide deep in the valley of this mountain. Due to her 'han' 한 [trauma, anger and/or injustice] her spirit was not at rest, and she would haunt this mountain. Some say that she brings misfortune to those disloyal,  greedy and abusive,  while she bestows blessings on those are kind, generous and good hearted. 
The story the shrine keeper told me goes a bit deeper. It was said due to her 'han' of injustice and pain, she would appear to the local villagers. Until her husband who felt so sorry for her and remorseful for what happened, enshrined her giving her offerings  and performing ceremony/ritual to help appease the spirit. (I dont know how true the next part is.....BUT)
It is said since then, that is when shamans [mudangs] started to incorporate and 'grab the ancestors' so that they may 'untie' the knots to release ancestrals 'han' and fury. ☀️🌙 I should add, that not every mudang can grab the ancestors,  its different than seeing or sensing an ancestor. To have the ability to 'grab' the ancestors spirit successfully...one must be born with the innate gift, and you also need a specific god deity for that task. Without theose two, it is seen as other mudang try and fumble around with the 'grabbing ancestors' part of the kut ceremony.

At the end of our session, I was gifted by her, a very sacred and strong tobacco that was given to her by another spiritworker.
