posts.caption:
What does it mean to be a Shaman?
How do you become a shaman? Well on the contrary to popular beliefs, its not something that you can take a "class" for, get an imaginary certificate from some shamanic insitute or teacher. This ancient art and practice isnt something that can be commercialized but yet it is insanely so. A shaman isnt a title that you can slap on like a Mickey D's name badge.
Yes, you can take a class to learn skills and techniques that you can apply to your own personal life. That doesnt mean you are a SHAMAN, it makes you a follower of shamanism. Its very crazy dangerous to mess with spirits when you dont have natural gifted talent. 
Becoming a shaman isnt a list of qualities or characteristics that you can check off on a list from Pinterest. Alot of shaman bloggers tend to write articles like 20 reason why you are a shaman or whatever bullshit they are feeding you. Just because you deal with shadow work in your reiki sessions, doesnt make you a shaman. Where there is light so is darkness..for gods sakes ppl! Its take more to be a shaman, than your personal beliefs and ego greed. 
There are only 2 ways of becoming a shaman, to be called upon the spirited shaman world. The first is to be marked or chosen by the spirits directly themselves. The second way is through blood lineage. 
To be marked or chosen, is like living a real nightmare. First the signs are subtle, but the more you ignore the calling the worse your life gets. Leads to a divine sickness, a shaman sickness that nothing can cure. The sickness is directly from the spirits causing you alot of pain and grief, and moments of mental unstability. 
I'm upset, I went through hell and back to get to this point in my life. I ran away from this calling only to be met with more grief and distress until I finally had to embrace the spirits.  I had to be broken down bit by bit, until I was left barely feeling alive. 
Then comes those who comes from privledge world, thinking this shit is the new trend. Being a shaman, travelling to Peru, or learning to journey  or has become the new "it" thing to do.

posts.caption:
Mala beads. A very sacred tool for many different cultures, tied with buddhism. 
Since our shamanic culture traditions and beliefs are intertwined with Buddhism, I use my mala beads all the time. Its very sacred, to use in prayer, meditation and to help keep count of the 108 prostrations. 
I see alot of "spiritual" or "bohemian" people, selling fancy mala beads using  swanky crystals. Its not what the beads are made from that gives you peace, its how you use it. And its not a jewelry accessory!!! Long ago, mala beads were made by monks...made from wood like the sacred pine tree or sandalwood because it has deep meanings. I get a little sad, or disheartened when I see people making profits off of other sacred cultural traditions. The lack of respect is what bothers me. 
Use the beads because of what it can do for you, use it as a tool to help you walk in the path of light. But to use fancy ass crystals, with tied-dyed tassel and retailing it for 80 bucks is disgusting to me. Yes it looks very bedazzling and purrrty, but like I said...please respect traditions and the very sacred beliefs. 😊 Thank you xoxo

posts.caption:
수성당 (Su seong dang)
A temple for Gaeyang Grandma and her 8 sisters who rules the west sea. Gaeyang grandma is the god of the sea and she walks the west sea, controlling the wind and the waves helping fisherman make huge catches of fish. She also helps and warns the fishermen of dangerous places while filling up the deepest parts of the ocean. 
The temple was originally built 1801 but reconstructed in 1996, villagers in this region holds memorial on the first day of the New Year. This temple is a cultural property protected by the government.  Tangible Cultural Property No. 58 
This majestic temple sits up on the hilltop, overlooking the vast ocean. On my pilgrimage we stopped by here to pray, put up offerings, had a mini ceremony and received ki (energy) 
How I would of loved to live here... listening to the wind, looking at the sky and talking to the ocean.

posts.caption:
I had the pleasure and honor of being asked by the editor of Sacred Hoops Magazine to write about muism and my personal journey into the world of mugyo. 
Korean shamanism mugyo isnt well known, as most mudang manshin shamans dont frequently service outside of their own culture. When I first felt my own calling, Ive thought about travelling into South America to meet with a shaman to learn, but more and more I felt pulled into my ancestral culture. I feel different, like a bridge to fill the gap between my two culture being American and Korean. 
Korean shamanism scared the shit out of me, it seemed more abrasive and harsher than other cultures. Shamans dancing on giant butcher knives, performing exorcism and acting all crazy gave me so much fear. But despite my fear, I was fated to meet an amazing teacher who held my hand and believed in my gifts. I forever indebted to my spirit mother, for she gave me a new life and breath in my lungs. 
Im still debating if I should write an article, its very humbling and at the same time stressful as I am sure not many articles are written about mugyo muism. This is my chance to voice my cultural heritage, and Im sure this opportunity isnt just a coincidence...

posts.caption:
My temple, my home, where I serve my gods, deities and ancestral spirits. My sacred space and my altar. 
Most wont understand the new lifestyle I need to adopt and live. Even I, struggle with my duties and responsibilities as a Mudang priestess. 
Every morning, I pour water in the bowls for my gods and deities. Light a candle and incense, grab my sacred sandalwood mala beads. Lay my mat on the floor, and I do full body 108 bows...twice a day. With every bow that I do, I pray humbly and mindfully. I am grateful, eternally grateful and then I meditate.  On special days, we prepare offerings and set the altar up for small feast. 
This duty of mine takes alot of my free time, I don't live the normal life of a NYC 32 year old. I dont have time for friends, a night out of fun. I have my duties and I will fulfill them earnestly. Forever grateful.

Image taken from Google.
This is the god Daesin Halmoni (대신할머니). Daesin means Great Spirit, Halmoni means grandmother. This god helps with fortune telling, notice her bell rattles, rice, fan and old coins used for divination.
I remember my first vision, I was sitting on the couch at a friends house. I just closed my eyes for a split second to practice my breathwork meditation. Then like watching a movie, unable to move. I saw my grandmother, she appeared and she took my hand flew up towards the sky. I looked back as I left my family behind as heartbroken as I was, I willingly followed as she lead me to the sky. We flew up up up, high above the sky and clouds. Silently I paid my respects to all my family elders and said my goodbye as I was leaving. 
My grandmother took me on this woodland path, and there were fields of golden rice on both sides of a dirt road. The rice fields were shining brightly, and then she took me inside a cave where a huge figure sat in the dark. He was massively bigger than us, my grandmother immediately started to bow down but I was confused.  Who is he, or she? Looked like an ancient king of sorts.
Months later, that vision came true. In the October, I flew to korea leaving my family behind embarking on a sacred pilgrimage back to my ancestral land.  There while travelling in the countryside where vast golden fields of rice ready for harvest. In the mountains, I had my initiation where I am forever committed to my gods and deities.

Patjuk is a red bean porridge traditionally eaten on the day of winter solstice.
The color red symbolizes positive energy and will chase negativity in my culture. 
Red bean also chases away evil spirits.
The story goes that there was a man named Gong Gong who had a terrible bad son. When the son died, he became the god of epidemic diseases killing alot of people.  When trying to search for a cure, they remembered the son of Gong Gong hated red bean porridge, so they began to place a bowl in every room of the house to chase away bad spirits and bad negative energy. 
Since then us (koreans) places patjuk everwhere in the house.

posts.caption:
Korean 장구 (Janggu)
I remember the first time my teacher used this #drum to chant our prayers. I felt out of place, foreign to this #ancient practice but yet comfortable as the sounds pierced through my being. 
Just then as I looked up at the paintings of our #ancestral gods/deities. Trying to pray, but instead I saw an exact image of Buddha pop out of his painting. The other shamans surrounded me, sensing my difficulties and emotions as tears dropped.
